# Basic Properties and Information Theory of Audic-Claverie Statistic for Analyzing cDNA Arrays 

## Peter Tiˇ no ∗1

> 1School of Computer Science, The University of Birmingham, Birmingham, B15 2TT, UK Email: Peter Tiˇ no ∗- P.Tino@cs.bham.co.uk;
> ∗Corresponding author

## Abstract 

Background: The Audic-Claverie method [1] has been and still continues to be a popular approach for detection of differentially expressed genes in the SAGE framework. The method is based on the assumption that under the null hypothesis tag counts of the same gene in two libraries come from the same but unknown Poisson distribution. The problem is that each SAGE library represents only a single measurement. We ask: Given that the tag count samples from SAGE libraries are extremely limited, how useful actually is the Audic-Claverie methodology? We rigorously analyze the A-C statistic that forms a backbone of the methodology and represents our knowledge of the underlying tag generating process based on one observation. 

Results: We show that the A-C statistic and the underlying Poisson distribution of the tag counts share the same mode structure. Moreover, the K-L divergence from the true unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic is minimized when the A-C statistic is conditioned on the mode of the Poisson distribution. Most importantly, the expectation of this K-L divergence never exceeds 1/2 bit. 

Conclusions: A rigorous underpinning of the Audic-Claverie methodology has been missing. Our results constitute a rigorous argument supporting the use of Audic-Claverie method even though the SAGE libraries represent very sparse samples. 

1Background 

It is of utmost importance for biologists to be able to analyze patterns of expression levels of selected genes in different tissues possibly obtained under different conditions or treatment regimes. Even subtle changes in gene expression levels can be indicators of biologically crucial processes such as cell differentiation and cell specialization [2]. Measurement of gene expression levels can be performed either via hybridization to microarrays, or by counting gene tags (signatures) using e.g. Serial Analysis of Gene Expression (SAGE) [3] or Massively Parallel Signature Sequencing (MPSS) [4] methodologies. The SAGE procedure results in a library of short sequence tags, each representing an expressed gene. The key assumption is that every mRNA copy in the tissue has the same chance of ending up as a tag in the library. Selecting a specific tag from the pool of transcripts can be approximately considered as sampling with replacement. The key step in many SAGE studies is identification of “interesting” genes, typically those that are differentially expressed under different conditions/treatments. This is done by comparing the number of specific tags found in the two SAGE libraries corresponding to different conditions or treatments. Several statistical tests have been suggested for identifying differentially expressed genes through comparing such digital expression profiles, e.g. [1, 2, 5, 6]. Audic and Claverie [1] were among the first to systematically study the influence of random fluctuations and sampling size on the reliability of digital expression profile data. Typically, cDNA libraries contain a large number of different expressed genes and observing a given cDNA qualifies as a rare event [1]. For a transcript representing a small fraction of the library and a large number N of clones, the probability of observing x tags of the same gene will be well-approximated by the Poisson distribution parametrized by

When comparing two libraries, it is assumed that under the null hypothesis of not differentially expressed genes the tag count x in one library comes from the same underlying Poisson distribution P (·| λ) as the tag count y in the other library. However, each SAGE library represents a single measurement only. From a purely statistical standpoint resolving this issue is potentially quite problematic. One can be excused for being rather skeptical about how much can actually be learned about the underlying unknown Poisson distribution from a single observation. Audic and Claverie [1] point out that this is a desirable property, since if the counts x, y are related to two libraries of the same size, they should be interchangeable when analyzing whether they come from the same underlying process or not. The A-C statistic ˜P (y|x) can be used e.g. for principled inferences, construction of confidence intervals, statistical testing etc. For further details regarding the derivation and mathematical treatment of the A-C statistic see [1]. Even though there have been further developments in comparison techniques for cDNA libraries (e.g. while Audic and Claverie [1] only deal with two libraries, Stekel et al. [7] suggest an approach to compare gene expressions across multiple cDNA libraries; for links to further approaches see [2]), the Audic-Claverie method has been and still continues to be a popular approach in current biological research, e.g. [8–17], with 427 citations 1, over 100 citations in the past 3 years. Given the widespread use of the Audic-Claverie method, it is somewhat surprising that a rigorous underpinning of the methodology has not yet been fully developed. Audic and Claverie did demonstrate the desirable behavior of their method through Monte Carlo simulations randomly sampling tags based on two experimentally obtained sequence tag distributions [1]. The rate of false alarm 2 was small for genes associated with small tag counts and increased for higher tag counts, but never exceeded the significance level of the test. Of course, one may argue that false alarm rate (false positives) is only one side of the story and ideally one would like to minimize both the false positive and false negative 3 rates. However, of equal importance is the issue of why the Audic-Claverie approach seems to be well-behaved, e.g. when compared to an approach based on Ricker’s confidence intervals (see [1]). In this contribution, we provide rigorous arguments as to why the Audic-Claverie method can be expected to work well, even though from the purely statistical standpoint

We then go beyond simple Monte-Carlo-style verification by rigorously studying how much and in what form can be actually learned about the distribution in the Audic-Claverie framework, given a single observation provided by a SAGE library. Basic properties of the A-C statistic

# The Significance of Digital Gene Expression Profiles 

# Ste ´phane Audic and Jean-Michel Claverie 1Laboratory of Structural and Genetic Information, Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique–E.P.91, Marseille 13402, France 

Genes differentially expressed in different tissues, during development, or during specific pathologies are of foremost interest to both basic and pharmaceutical research. ‘‘Transcript profiles’’ or ‘‘digital Northerns’’ are generated routinely by partially sequencing thousands of randomly selected clones from relevant cDNA libraries. Differentially expressed genes can then be detected from variations in the counts of their cognate sequence tags. Here we present the first systematic study on the influence of random fluctuations and sampling size on the reliability of this kind of data. We establish a rigorous significance test and demonstrate its use on publicly available transcript profiles. The theory links the threshold of selection of putatively regulated genes (e.g., the number of pharmaceutical leads) to the fraction of false positive clones one is willing to risk. Our results delineate more precisely and extend the limits within which digital Northern data can be used. 

Very large-scale, single-pass partial sequencing of cDNA clones from a large number of libraries has led to the identification of ∼50,000 human genes (Ad-ams et al. 1995; Aaronson et al. 1996; Hillier et al. 1996). However, a precise function or a complete transcript sequence are known for <5000 of these (Adams et al. 1995; Boguski and Schuler 1995). In the absence of functional clues for most of the newly identified genes, evidence of differential ex-pression is the most important criteria to prioritize the exploitation of anonymous sequence data in both basic and pharmaceutical (Nowak 1995; Ad-ams 1996; Bains 1996; Editorial 1996) research. For example, the study of expression profiles in various tumors is central to the new Cancer Genome Anatomy project (Kuska 1996; O’Brien 1997). In contrast to functional assays, the quantitative analysis of gene expression level lends itself to large-scale implementation. Two main approaches have been proposed (1) ‘‘analog’’ methods based on hy-bridization to arrayed cDNA libraries (Lennon and Lehrach 1991; Gress et al. 1992; Nguyen et al. 1995; Schena et al. 1995; Zhao et al. 1995) or oligonucleo-tide ‘‘chips’’ (Fodor et al. 1991; Southern et al. 1992; Guo et al. 1994; Matson et al. 1995); and (2) ‘‘digi-tal’’ methods, based on the generation of sequence tags. This paper focuses on the latter. The sequence tag-based method (Okubo et al. 1992; Matsubara and Okubo 1994) consists of generating a large number (thousands) of expressed sequence tags (ESTs) (Adams et al. 1991; Wilcox et al. 1991; Adams et al. 1992; Khan et al. 1992) from 3 8-directed re-gional non-normalized cDNA libraries. Recently, Velculescu et al. (1995) have introduced the serial analysis of gene expression (SAGE). Although tags are 100–300 nucleotides in length in the original EST approach, the SAGE method only requires nine nucleotides, therefore allowing a larger throughput. In both protocols, the number of tags is reported to be proportional to the abundance of cognate tran-scripts in the tissue or cell type used to make the cDNA library. The variation in the relative fre-quency of those tags, stored in computer databases, is then used to point out the differential expression of the corresponding genes: This is the concept of a ‘‘digital Northern’’ comparison. In the absence of a sound theoretical framework, the validity of the method has only been verified for a handful of genes in the context of two cellular differentiation systems (Lee et al. 1995; Okubo et al. 1995) induc-ible in vitro. Yet, with a total number of human genes of ∼80,000 or more, it is not intuitive that sequencing a mere few thousand tags (a typical ex-periment) from highly redundant non-normalized cDNA libraries can produce a useful picture, or real-istic ‘‘transcript profile,’’ of a given tissue, develop-ment stage, or cell type. What variations in tag numbers allow for a reliable inference about differ-ential expression? How many tags should be gener-ated? Here we present the statistical framework re-quired to answer those questions and analyze tran-script profiles in a quantitative manner.

RESULTS 

In Methods we establish the probability distribution governing the occurrence of the same rare event in duplicate experiments. This probability distribution is a general result applicable to a wide variety of experimental situations, although this paper fo-cuses on its use to analyze digital gene expression patterns. The main and only mathematical assump-tion behind the derivation is that the observed events are rare and part of a large population of possible outcomes (the distribution of which is not specified). In the context of a digital Northern, one event is the observation of a given cDNA sequence tag, and the experiment consists of the random picking and partial sequencing of a number N of cDNA clones. Given the usual complexity (i.e., the number of different genes expressed) of cDNA li-braries, observing a given cDNA qualifies as a rare event, as the abundance of most individual mes-sages is of the order of a few percents or less. 

Random Fluctuation vs. Significant Change in Tag Number: When to Infer Differential Expression 

Let us randomly pick N = 1000 clones from a cDNA library and generate the corresponding sequence tags; a given message (e.g., interleukin-2) will be picked x (e.g., two) times, with x in a typical (0–10) range. If we now redo this experiment, that is, again pick 1000 clones and generate the tags, the same message will now be picked y (e.g., 3) times. If the experiments have been duplicated correctly and the clones selected at random, we expect x and y to be close, albeit often different because of random fluc-tuations. In the Methods section, we show that the expected probability of observing y occurrences of a clone already observed x times is given by the simple formula: 

p(y|x) = ~x + y!!

x!y!2 ~x + y + 1! (1) Equation 1 can be used to compute a confi-dence interval [ymin, ymax] e within which we expect to find y with a given probability, noted 1–2 e, where 2e is the significance level. For e small (e.g., 2.5% or less), y values falling outside the [ymin, ymax] e inter-val correspond to p(y | x) << 1, therefore pointing out very unlikely random fluctuations between the two experiments. The confidence intervals for the usual 1% and 5% significance levels are given in Table 1. The same confidence intervals listed in Table 1 can in fact be used to analyze the results of sampling 

N clones from two different libraries. Provided all experimental factors are well replicated, significant discrepancies between x (from one library) and y

(from the other) will now characterize differentially expressed genes, for example, the relative abun-dance of which is unlikely to be the same in the two libraries. Simply reading Table 1, we see that varia-tions in counts such as 7 → 0, or 2 → 12 are signifi-cant ( P < 0.01) evidence of regulated gene expres-sion, whereas variations such as 3 → 0 or 8 → 16 are not ( P > 0.05). However, we do not advocate the use of rigid significance thresholds to analyze digital transcript profiles, as discussed below. 

Influence of the Sampling Size 

Surprisingly at first, p(y | x) in Equation 1 does not involve the sampling size N, that is, the total num-ber of picked clones. The fluctuation probabilities, and confidence intervals, depend only on the values of the observed counts. To understand why, we must remember that Equation 1 governs the results of strictly duplicated experiments. Given N clones are sampled, the most likely tags to be picked up are, intuitively, those corresponding to cDNA, the abun-dance of which is of the order of 1/ N, or larger (ac-cording to Equation 3, the probability of finding a given cDNA with 1/ N abundance while picking up 

N clones is 0.63, see also Equation 13). Choosing a sampling size therefore corresponds to targeting a given subset of genes, the level of expression of which allows their tags to occur at reasonable fre-quencies. As expected, more reliable inferences can be made on clones corresponding to larger absolute frequencies (i.e., the ones more often picked up). For example (see Table 1), a variation in counts from 1–3 (threefold increase) is not indicative of a signifi-cant ( P < 0.05) increase, whereas a variation from 4–12 is significant at P < 0.05, and a variation from 7–21 is significant at P < 0.01. For a gene expressed at a given rate, increasing the sampling size N leads to higher tag counts, and allows more stringent sta-tistical inference to be made, for the same propor-tional variation. Most often in practice one wishes to compare digital Northerns or gene profiles that have been computed from the random picking of different numbers of clones, N1 and N2. The mathematical problem is now to establish the probability for a given cDNA (e.g., interleukin-2) to be picked up x

times when the sampling size was N1 and y times when the sampling size was N2. Equation 1 then becomes (see Methods):

In practice, Equation 2 will be used to analyze experiments per-formed on two different libraries, using different sampling sizes. For the same expression level, larger N will result in larger absolute values for x and y, making the detection of significant differential expression more sensitive.

The (2 2 2) contingency tables arising from treat-ment versus control experiments are traditionally analyzed with Fisher’s exact test (Siegel 1956; Agresti 1996). Differential EST count data can be presented in a tabulated form so as to suggest the use of this test, as follows: 

Brain cDNA library Liver cDNA library Number of actin ESTs 2 11 Number of other ESTs 998 1189 Total clones sampled 1000 1200 

The statistical significance according to Fisher’s exact test for such a result is 4.6% (two-tail 

P-value, i.e., the probability for such a table to occur in the hypothesis that actin EST frequencies are in-dependent of the cDNA libraries). In comparison, the P-value computed from the cumulative form (Equation 9, see Methods) of Equation 2 (i.e., for the relative frequency of actin ESTs to be the same in both libraries, given that at least 11 cognate ESTs are observed in the liver library after two were observed in the brain library) is 1.6%. Fisher’s (2 2 2) exact test is always more conservative than our test (e.g., Fisher’s P-value of 1.6% requires a 2 → 13 EST count transition in the above setting). Besides being too conservative, there is a more fundamental difficulty in using this test to analyze EST count data. The sampling scheme assumed by Fisher’s exact test in principle requires the total number of data values in the contingency table to be fixed, as well as both the row marginal total and the column marginal totals. In our prospective experimental situation, only the column marginals (i.e., the numbers of clones sampled from each library) are fixed. The extension of Fisher’s exact test to cases where only one set of marginal totals is fixed (Tocher 1950) is still contro-versial. In the context of the above EST counting results, there is an additional problem with the lack of homogeneity in the definition of the ‘‘other EST’’ category. This category represents different subsets of transcripts for different libraries. The use of Fisher’s (2 2 2) exact test is more natural for a different type of EST data analysis: the study of library-dependent alternative transcripts of the same gene (i.e., splice or polyadenylation vari-ants) (D. Gautheret, O. Poirot, F. Lopez, S. Audic, and J.-M. Claverie, in prep.). Here, the results for an hypothetical gene G1 may look as follows: 

G1-related transcripts in brain library G1-related transcripts in liver library Long-form mRNA 2 10 Short-form mRNA 8 3Total G1-related clones 10 13 

where the alternative categories are unambiguously defined and refer to the same objects. For example, the above results constitute good evidence that G1 is expressed in different forms in those tissues (Fisher’s exact test two-tail P-value = 1.2%). 

False Leads in the Selection of Candidate Genes 

A crucial measure of the power of statistical signifi-cance tests is their rate of false alarm, that is, how often random fluctuations are expected to be mis-taken for significant differences in the results. When analyzing the transcript profiles from two different libraries, a false alarm would cause a gene to be deemed differentially transcribed, whereas in fact it is not. The rate of false alarm is therefore a direct estimate of the fraction of false leads, when search-ing for differentially expressed genes on the basis of differences in tag counts. The rates of false alarm associated with the P < 0.01 and P < 0.05 confi-dence intervals listed in Table 1 have been com-puted by Monte-Carlo simulation on the basis of two experimental sequence tag distributions (Table 2; Fig. 1). The rate of false alarms associated with the use of Equation 1 (in fact, its cumulative form Equa-tion 9, see Methods) is very small for genes repre-sented by small tag counts and slowly increases for higher tag counts, without ever exceeding the se-lected significance level. Such good behavior vali-dates the use of the confidence intervals (Table 1) computed from Equation 1 and Equation 9 to assess the statistical significance of variations in digital Northern data. The curves labeled ‘‘window’’ char-acterize the very similar behavior of a slightly less conservative derivation of the same test (see Meth-ods, Equation 15). For comparison, Figure 1 also presents the behavior of another test, based on an inappropriate application of Ricker’s confidence in-tervals (Ricker 1937) (see Methods). 

DISCUSSION 

An appropriate statistical test is now at our disposal to begin analyzing digital gene expression profiles

For example, the test can be used to determine how many genes appear regulated at various confidence levels using the data from a typical experiment (e.g., sampling a thou-sand clones). We analyzed the data gathered by Okubo et al. (1995) on the human promyelocytic leukemia cell line HL60 induced by dimethylsulfox-ide (DMSO) or tetradecanoylphorbolacetate (TPA). Table 3 shows the 21 EST classes the occurrences of which exhibit significant variations at the 1% level. Most of the corresponding genes make biological sense in term of differentiation along the granulo-cyte or monocyte pathways. This example serves to discuss a subtle point in the interpretation of the P values computed from Equation 1, 2, and 9. Rigorously, these equations apply to the case where a given gene (e.g., lipocor-tin) would have been selected for scrutiny before looking at the differences in cognate tag counts be-tween libraries. For example, the study of expression profiles in various tumors is central to the new Cancer Genome Anatomy project (Kuska 1996; O’Brien 1997). In contrast to functional assays, the quantitative analysis of gene expression level lends itself to large-scale implementation. Two main approaches have been proposed (1) ‘‘analog’’ methods based on hy-bridization to arrayed cDNA libraries (Lennon and Lehrach 1991; Gress et al. 1992; Nguyen et al. 1995; Schena et al. 1995; Zhao et al. 1995) or oligonucleo-tide ‘‘chips’’ (Fodor et al. 1991; Southern et al. 1992; Guo et al. 1994; Matson et al. 1995); and (2) ‘‘digi-tal’’ methods, based on the generation of sequence tags. This paper focuses on the latter. The sequence tag-based method (Okubo et al. 1992; Matsubara and Okubo 1994) consists of generating a large number (thousands) of expressed sequence tags (ESTs) (Adams et al. 1991; Wilcox et al. 1991; Adams et al. 1992; Khan et al. 1992) from 3 8-directed re-gional non-normalized cDNA libraries. Recently, Velculescu et al. (1995) have introduced the serial analysis of gene expression (SAGE). Although tags are 100–300 nucleotides in length in the original EST approach, the SAGE method only requires nine nucleotides, therefore allowing a larger throughput. In both protocols, the number of tags is reported to be proportional to the abundance of cognate tran-scripts in the tissue or cell type used to make the cDNA library. The variation in the relative fre-quency of those tags, stored in computer databases, is then used to point out the differential expression of the corresponding genes: This is the concept of a ‘‘digital Northern’’ comparison. In the absence of a sound theoretical framework, the validity of the method has only been verified for a handful of genes in the context of two cellular differentiation systems (Lee et al. 1995; Okubo et al. 1995) induc-ible in vitro. Yet, with a total number of human genes of ∼80,000 or more, it is not intuitive that sequencing a mere few thousand tags (a typical ex-periment) from highly redundant non-normalized cDNA libraries can produce a useful picture, or real-istic ‘‘transcript profile,’’ of a given tissue, develop-ment stage, or cell type. What variations in tag numbers allow for a reliable inference about differ-ential expression? How many tags should be gener-ated? Here we present the statistical framework re-quired to answer those questions and analyze tran-script profiles in a quantitative manner.

RESULTS 

In Methods we establish the probability distribution governing the occurrence of the same rare event in duplicate experiments. This probability distribution is a general result applicable to a wide variety of experimental situations, although this paper fo-cuses on its use to analyze digital gene expression patterns. The main and only mathematical assump-tion behind the derivation is that the observed events are rare and part of a large population of possible outcomes (the distribution of which is not specified). In the context of a digital Northern, one event is the observation of a given cDNA sequence tag, and the experiment consists of the random picking and partial sequencing of a number N of cDNA clones. Given the usual complexity (i.e., the number of different genes expressed) of cDNA li-braries, observing a given cDNA qualifies as a rare event, as the abundance of most individual mes-sages is of the order of a few percents or less. 

Random Fluctuation vs. Significant Change in Tag Number: When to Infer Differential Expression 

Let us randomly pick N = 1000 clones from a cDNA library and generate the corresponding sequence tags; a given message (e.g., interleukin-2) will be picked x (e.g., two) times, with x in a typical (0–10) range. If we now redo this experiment, that is, again pick 1000 clones and generate the tags, the same message will now be picked y (e.g., 3) times. If the experiments have been duplicated correctly and the clones selected at random, we expect x and y to be close, albeit often different because of random fluc-tuations. In the Methods section, we show that the expected probability of observing y occurrences of a clone already observed x times is given by the simple formula:

Influence of the Sampling Size 

Surprisingly at first, p(y | x) in Equation 1 does not involve the sampling size N, that is, the total num-ber of picked clones. The fluctuation probabilities, and confidence intervals, depend only on the values of the observed counts. To understand why, we must remember that Equation 1 governs the results of strictly duplicated experiments. Given N clones are sampled, the most likely tags to be picked up are, intuitively, those corresponding to cDNA, the abun-dance of which is of the order of 1/ N, or larger (ac-cording to Equation 3, the probability of finding a given cDNA with 1/ N abundance while picking up 

N clones is 0.63, see also Equation 13). Choosing a sampling size therefore corresponds to targeting a given subset of genes, the level of expression of which allows their tags to occur at reasonable fre-quencies. As expected, more reliable inferences can be made on clones corresponding to larger absolute frequencies (i.e., the ones more often picked up). For example (see Table 1), a variation in counts from 1–3 (threefold increase) is not indicative of a signifi-cant ( P < 0.05) increase, whereas a variation from 4–12 is significant at P < 0.05, and a variation from 7–21 is significant at P < 0.01. For a gene expressed at a given rate, increasing the sampling size N leads to higher tag counts, and allows more stringent sta-tistical inference to be made, for the same propor-tional variation. Most often in practice one wishes to compare digital Northerns or gene profiles that have been computed from the random picking of different numbers of clones, N1 and N2. The mathematical problem is now to establish the probability for a given cDNA (e.g., interleukin-2) to be picked up x

The (2 2 2) contingency tables arising from treat-ment versus control experiments are traditionally analyzed with Fisher’s exact test (Siegel 1956; Agresti 1996). Differential EST count data can be presented in a tabulated form so as to suggest the use of this test, as follows: 

Brain cDNA library Liver cDNA library Number of actin ESTs 2 11 Number of other ESTs 998 1189 Total clones sampled 1000 1200 

The statistical significance according to Fisher’s exact test for such a result is 4.6% (two-tail 

P-value, i.e., the probability for such a table to occur in the hypothesis that actin EST frequencies are in-dependent of the cDNA libraries). In comparison, the P-value computed from the cumulative form (Equation 9, see Methods) of Equation 2 (i.e., for the relative frequency of actin ESTs to be the same in both libraries, given that at least 11 cognate ESTs are observed in the liver library after two were observed in the brain library) is 1.6%. Fisher’s (2 2 2) exact test is always more conservative than our test (e.g., Fisher’s P-value of 1.6% requires a 2 → 13 EST count transition in the above setting). Besides being too conservative, there is a more fundamental difficulty in using this test to analyze EST count data. The sampling scheme assumed by Fisher’s exact test in principle requires the total number of data values in the contingency table to be fixed, as well as both the row marginal total and the column marginal totals. In our prospective experimental situation, only the column marginals (i.e., the numbers of clones sampled from each library) are fixed. The extension of Fisher’s exact test to cases where only one set of marginal totals is fixed (Tocher 1950) is still contro-versial. In the context of the above EST counting results, there is an additional problem with the lack of homogeneity in the definition of the ‘‘other EST’’ category. This category represents different subsets of transcripts for different libraries. The use of Fisher’s (2 2 2) exact test is more natural for a different type of EST data analysis: the study of library-dependent alternative transcripts of the same gene (i.e., splice or polyadenylation vari-ants) (D. Gautheret, O. Poirot, F. Lopez, S. Audic, and J.-M. Claverie, in prep.). Here, the results for an hypothetical gene G1 may look as follows:

False Leads in the Selection of Candidate Genes 

A crucial measure of the power of statistical signifi-cance tests is their rate of false alarm, that is, how often random fluctuations are expected to be mis-taken for significant differences in the results. When analyzing the transcript profiles from two different libraries, a false alarm would cause a gene to be deemed differentially transcribed, whereas in fact it is not. The rate of false alarm is therefore a direct estimate of the fraction of false leads, when search-ing for differentially expressed genes on the basis of differences in tag counts. The rates of false alarm associated with the P < 0.01 and P < 0.05 confi-dence intervals listed in Table 1 have been com-puted by Monte-Carlo simulation on the basis of two experimental sequence tag distributions (Table 2; Fig. 1). The rate of false alarms associated with the use of Equation 1 (in fact, its cumulative form Equa-tion 9, see Methods) is very small for genes repre-sented by small tag counts and slowly increases for higher tag counts, without ever exceeding the se-lected significance level. Such good behavior vali-dates the use of the confidence intervals (Table 1) computed from Equation 1 and Equation 9 to assess the statistical significance of variations in digital Northern data. The curves labeled ‘‘window’’ char-acterize the very similar behavior of a slightly less conservative derivation of the same test (see Meth-ods, Equation 15). For comparison, Figure 1 also presents the behavior of another test, based on an inappropriate application of Ricker’s confidence in-tervals (Ricker 1937) (see Methods).

In con-trast, and thanks to the unique properties of the Poisson distribution, digital methods have the ca-pacity of providing a quantitative assessment of dif-ferential expression without the repetition or the standardization of individual tag-counting experi-ments. The statistical analysis presented here pro-vides an objective method to analyze digital tran-script profile data, and adapts it to fit (1) the num-ber of leads one wants to be followed; (2) the fraction of false clues to be tolerated; and (3) the level of modulation in gene expression considered of biological interest. # Basic Properties and Information Theory of Audic-Claverie Statistic for Analyzing cDNA Arrays 

## Peter Tiˇ no ∗1

> 1School of Computer Science, The University of Birmingham, Birmingham, B15 2TT, UK Email: Peter Tiˇ no ∗- P.Tino@cs.bham.co.uk;
> ∗Corresponding author

## Abstract 

Background: The Audic-Claverie method [1] has been and still continues to be a popular approach for detection of differentially expressed genes in the SAGE framework. The method is based on the assumption that under the null hypothesis tag counts of the same gene in two libraries come from the same but unknown Poisson distribution. The problem is that each SAGE library represents only a single measurement. We ask: Given that the tag count samples from SAGE libraries are extremely limited, how useful actually is the Audic-Claverie methodology? We rigorously analyze the A-C statistic that forms a backbone of the methodology and represents our knowledge of the underlying tag generating process based on one observation. 

Results: We show that the A-C statistic and the underlying Poisson distribution of the tag counts share the same mode structure. Moreover, the K-L divergence from the true unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic is minimized when the A-C statistic is conditioned on the mode of the Poisson distribution. Most importantly, the expectation of this K-L divergence never exceeds 1/2 bit. 

Conclusions: A rigorous underpinning of the Audic-Claverie methodology has been missing. Our results constitute a rigorous argument supporting the use of Audic-Claverie method even though the SAGE libraries represent very sparse samples. 

1Background 

It is of utmost importance for biologists to be able to analyze patterns of expression levels of selected genes in different tissues possibly obtained under different conditions or treatment regimes. Even subtle changes in gene expression levels can be indicators of biologically crucial processes such as cell differentiation and cell specialization [2]. Measurement of gene expression levels can be performed either via hybridization to microarrays, or by counting gene tags (signatures) using e.g. Serial Analysis of Gene Expression (SAGE) [3] or Massively Parallel Signature Sequencing (MPSS) [4] methodologies. The SAGE procedure results in a library of short sequence tags, each representing an expressed gene. The key assumption is that every mRNA copy in the tissue has the same chance of ending up as a tag in the library. Selecting a specific tag from the pool of transcripts can be approximately considered as sampling with replacement. The key step in many SAGE studies is identification of “interesting” genes, typically those that are differentially expressed under different conditions/treatments. This is done by comparing the number of specific tags found in the two SAGE libraries corresponding to different conditions or treatments. Several statistical tests have been suggested for identifying differentially expressed genes through comparing such digital expression profiles, e.g. [1, 2, 5, 6]. Audic and Claverie [1] were among the first to systematically study the influence of random fluctuations and sampling size on the reliability of digital expression profile data. Typically, cDNA libraries contain a large number of different expressed genes and observing a given cDNA qualifies as a rare event [1]. For a transcript representing a small fraction of the library and a large number N of clones, the probability of observing x tags of the same gene will be well-approximated by the Poisson distribution parametrized by 

λ ≥ 0:

When comparing two libraries, it is assumed that under the null hypothesis of not differentially expressed genes the tag count x in one library comes from the same underlying Poisson distribution P (·| λ) as the tag count y in the other library. However, each SAGE library represents a single measurement only. From a purely statistical standpoint resolving this issue is potentially quite problematic. One can be excused for being rather skeptical about how much can actually be learned about the underlying unknown Poisson distribution from a single observation. The key instrument of the Audic-Claverie approach is a distribution ˜P (y|x) over tag counts y in one library 2informed by the tag count x in the other library, under the null hypothesis that the tag counts are generated from the same but unknown Poisson distribution. ˜P (y|x) is obtained by Bayesian averaging (infinite mixture) of all possible Poisson distributions P (y|λ′) with mixing proportions equal to the posteriors p(λ′|x) under the flat prior over λ. Audic and Claverie [1] point out that this is a desirable property, since if the counts x, y are related to two libraries of the same size, they should be interchangeable when analyzing whether they come from the same underlying process or not. The A-C statistic ˜P (y|x) can be used e.g. for principled inferences, construction of confidence intervals, statistical testing etc. For further details regarding the derivation and mathematical treatment of the A-C statistic see [1]. Even though there have been further developments in comparison techniques for cDNA libraries (e.g. while Audic and Claverie [1] only deal with two libraries, Stekel et al. [7] suggest an approach to compare gene expressions across multiple cDNA libraries; for links to further approaches see [2]), the Audic-Claverie method has been and still continues to be a popular approach in current biological research, e.g. [8–17], with 427 citations 1, over 100 citations in the past 3 years. Given the widespread use of the Audic-Claverie method, it is somewhat surprising that a rigorous underpinning of the methodology has not yet been fully developed. Audic and Claverie did demonstrate the desirable behavior of their method through Monte Carlo simulations randomly sampling tags based on two experimentally obtained sequence tag distributions [1]. The rate of false alarm 2 was small for genes associated with small tag counts and increased for higher tag counts, but never exceeded the significance level of the test. Of course, one may argue that false alarm rate (false positives) is only one side of the story and ideally one would like to minimize both the false positive and false negative 3 rates. However, of equal importance is the issue of why the Audic-Claverie approach seems to be well-behaved, e.g. when compared to an approach based on Ricker’s confidence intervals (see [1]). In this contribution, we provide rigorous arguments as to why the Audic-Claverie method can be expected to work well, even though from the purely statistical standpoint

Information theory of the A-C statistic 

We now answer, in the framework of information theory, the second question posed in the ‘Background’ section. Assume that there is some “true” underlying Poisson distribution P (y|λ) (1) over possible counts 6y ≥ 0 with unknown parameter λ. In the same process, we first generate a count x and then use the A-C statistic ˜P (y|x) (3) to define a distribution over y, given the already observed count x. We ask: How different, in terms of Kullback-Leibler (K-L) divergence, are the two distributions over y? For the A-C statistic to work, one would naturally like ˜P (y|x) to be sufficiently representative of the true unknown distribution P (y|λ). ## Results and Discussion 

The Audic-Claverie method [1] has been and still continues to be a popular approach for detection of differentially expressed genes in the SAGE framework. The problem is that each SAGE library represents only a single measurement. We have rigorously analyzed usefulness of the Audic-Claverie method by investigating the A-C statistic ˜P (y|x)that forms a backbone of the method and represents our knowledge of the underlying Poisson distribution 

P (·| λ) based on only one tag count x drawn from it. It turns out that the Poisson distribution is rather “rigid” in the sense that it is unimodal and parametrized by a single parameter λ representing both its mean and variance. Learning about P (·| λ) from a very limited sample (as one is effectively bound to do in the SAGE framework) is much less suspicious than one might naively expect. We have first shown that the A-C statistic ˜P (y|x), even though not a Poisson distribution itself, naturally captures the distribution of further tag counts y, given a single observation x from the unknown P (·| λ). According to Theorem 1, for integer λ, both ˜P (·| x) and P (·| λ) have two neighboring modes with decreasing probability values as one moves away from the modes in either direction. In particular, P (·| λ) has the modes located at λ and λ − 1, with P (λ|λ) = P (λ − 1|λ). Given a tag count x ≥ 1, ˜P (y|x) has the modes located at x and x − 1, with ˜P (x|x) = ˜P (x − 1|x). We then analyzed how ‘close’ is the A-C statistic ˜P (·| λ) (in terms of K-L divergence) to the underlying Poisson distribution P (·| λ) of tag counts. It turns out that the K-L divergence from P (y|λ) to ˜P (y|x) is 12 minimized at the mode of P (y|λ), i.e. when x = λ − 1 (Theorem 2). Most importantly, by Theorem 4, on average, the A-C statistic is never too far from the true underlying distribution. To be precise, up to terms of order O(λ−3), on average, the A-C statistic is never further away from the truth P (·| λ) than half-a-bit of additional information. Hence, the Audic-Claverie method can be expected to work well even though the SAGE libraries represent very sparse samples. So far the Audic-Claverie methodology for detection of differentially expressed genes has been verified only empirically through a series of specific Monte Carlo simulations [1]. It has not been clear how general the apparently stable simulation findings were. Besides detailed explanations of the nature of A-C statistic capturing the unknown Poisson distribution based on single observation only, we showed that the A-C statistic is universally applicable in any situation where inferences about the underlying Poisson distribution must be made based on an extremely sparse sample. Such situations are referred to in machine learning as ‘one-shot-learning’. In the Monte Carlo simulations of [1] the false alarm rate was small for genes associated with small tag counts and gradually increased for higher tag counts. The false alarm rate, however, never exceeded the significance level of the test. These findings are consistent with the theoretically calculated divergence function E(λ) (eq. (20)) illustrated in figure 2. With increasing mean tag count λ, it is more likely that increased counts x will be observed. But as λ increases, so does the uncertainty in the generating Poisson distribution P (·| λ). Consequently, the average K-L divergence E(λ)from P (·| λ) to the approximating A-C statistic (based on a single realization x from P (·| λ)) gets larger. For smaller λ the underlying Poisson distribution is well captured by the A-C statistic and the test that operates on it will be well behaved. As λ grows, the average K-L divergence E(λ) saturates at 0.5 bits implying that the test based on the A-C statistic will continue to be well behaved even for large values of the mean tag count λ.The Audic-Claverie method has also been formulated for the case of two cDNA libraries of unequal size. Similar methodologies have been proposed for the case of multiple cDNA libraries (e.g. [7]). Even though developed under the limited assumption of two libraries of the same size, theoretical results obtained in this paper offer deep insights into the workings of the Audic-Claverie approach and provide an information theoretic justification for its use when analyzing expression patterns in cDNA arrays. Of course, when using libraries of unequal size, the A-C statistic will no longer be symmetric, putting more weight on the more populated library. Information theoretic investigation of statistics developed for pattern analysis in the cases of unequal multiple libraries is a matter for our future work. 13 Conclusions 

Detection of differentially expressed genes is a crucial step in any large scale automated analysis of patterns of gene expression data. One of the most popular techniques for identifying genes with statistically different expression in SAGE libraries is the methodology of Audic and Claverie [1]. The methodology relies on learning the underlying Poisson distribution of tag counts from a single observation from it in the form of (A-C statistic). In this paper we rigorously analyzed the A-C statistic. We have shown that under the null hypothesis of not differentially expressed genes: 1. The A-C statistic and the underlying Poisson distribution share the same mode structure. 2. The K-L divergence from the true unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic is minimized when the A-C statistic is conditioned on the mode (not mean) of the Poisson distribution. 3. The expected K-L divergence from the true unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic is never larger than 1/2 bit, irrespective of the mean of the Poisson distribution. 4. The expected K-L divergence from the true unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic can be approximated up to order O(λ−3) by a simple function of the form a0 + a1λ−1 + a2λ−2. For the divergence measured in bits, a0 = 1 /2, a1 = 1 /24 and a2 = 1 /32. Even though the A-C statistic infers the unknown underlying Poisson distribution based on one count observation only, the Audic-Claverie method should work reasonably well in most cases, since under the null hypothesis, the average divergence from the unknown Poisson distribution to the A-C statistic is guaranteed not to exceed 1/2 bit. This constitutes a rigorous quantitative argument, extending the empirical Monte Carlo studies of [1], that supports the wide spread use of Audic-Claverie method, even though by their very nature, the SAGE libraries represent very sparse samples.

# SIC to NAICS Code Conversion

## SIC to NAICS Crosswalk - SIC to NAICS Code Mapping and Cross-Reference

For classification methodology and official mapping context, see the [SIC Classification & Reference Center](link_2).

## How to Convert SIC Codes to NAICS Codes

Enter a SIC code or keyword in the search box above to find the corresponding NAICS code or codes.

In some cases, a single SIC code may map to multiple NAICS codes. When this occurs, review the NAICS definitions and included or excluded activities to determine the best fit based on the establishment's primary activity.

## SIC to NAICS Crosswalk

The SIC to NAICS crosswalk provides a structured mapping between legacy SIC classifications and the modern NAICS system. Because the two systems differ in structure and scope, mappings are not always one-to-one. The crosswalk is intended to identify candidate NAICS codes that should be verified against official NAICS definitions.

## SIC to NAICS Conversion Table

After completing a search using the SIC to NAICS Conversion Tool, the results display SIC codes in the left column and mapped NAICS codes in the right column. Click any SIC or NAICS code in the table to open the detailed code page, where you can review definitions, hierarchy placement, and included or excluded activities.

Note: SIC-to-NAICS mappings are not always one-to-one. Final NAICS selection should be validated using official NAICS definitions and establishment-level classification rules.

# SIC Codes Lookup - Standard Industrial Classification

### Search or browse the Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) system. Verify the correct SIC code using definitions, scope boundaries, and industry hierarchy.

Search Keyword 

[What is a SIC Code](link_60)·[How to Find My SIC Code](link_61)·

Instructions

1.   Enter a SIC code or a keyword describing the business activity.
2.   Review matching SIC codes in the results list.
3.   Click a SIC code to view its definition, included activities, and industry scope.
4.   Choose the code that best represents the establishment's primary activity.

 Governed classification reference since 1998 · Full SIC coverage · Included/excluded boundary checks 

## What is the SIC Code Lookup / Directory?

The SIC Code Lookup / Directory on SICCODE.com offers a structured, research‑grade method for locating accurate 2‑ to 4‑digit SIC classifications. Users can search by keyword or known SIC code to surface potential matches, then validate the correct classification by reviewing industry definitions, scope notes, and the hierarchical placement within each major division. For guided exploration, begin with a major division and follow the hierarchy downward - from broad industry categories to the most specific 4‑digit SIC code.

### 🔹 Direct Lookup

Quickly identify SIC codes by entering a keyword or code number, then open the corresponding page to review definitions, scope boundaries, and classification notes.

### 🔹 Hierarchical Navigation

Start at the division level and move through major groups to reach the exact 4‑digit SIC code, following the original structure of the SIC system.

### 🔹 Standards‑Aligned Reference

Relies on authoritative SIC definitions and industry scope guidance to support accurate classification and reduce ambiguity.

### 🔹 Classification Governance Support

Applies primary‑activity principles and establishment‑level logic to help ensure consistent, defensible SIC code assignment across use cases.

## Browse SIC Code List

Start with the sector that best matches the establishment's primary activity, then narrow by business model and scope to reach the correct 4-digit SIC code.

## Website-Reviewed & Enriched

Get the companies that best match your target, not everyone in the industry. Specialists review each company website to identify products, services, markets, and fit.

1.   ### Tell us who you want to reach

Describe the companies, products, services, or use case. You do not need a NAICS or SIC code to start.

2.   ### Get your free count and sample

We recommend the mix of classifications, company data, and website research that fits your target, then send a count and sample.

3.   ### Approve and receive your list

Review your count, sample, scope, and quote. Once approved, we'll complete the review and deliver your list.

### Example: Commercial Plumbers

Your target is commercial plumbers, not every plumbing company.

Tell us that. We can use plumbing NAICS and SIC where they help, then review websites to keep commercial, industrial, municipal, emergency, drain-cleaning, and specialty shops, and leave out residential-only businesses where possible.

Commercial Industrial Municipal Mechanical Emergency Service Drain Cleaning Residential-Only Flag Specialty Services

### Is this included with every list?

A standard list uses industry codes and business filters. Website-Reviewed & Enriched is for when your target is more specific than a code: products, services, markets, and fit.

### Why is it a custom service?

Every buyer has a different target. One customer may want commercial plumbers, while another may want residential repair companies, suppliers, contractors, or specialty service providers.

### What does it improve?

Website-Reviewed & Enriched helps reduce noise. The goal is a cleaner list with more companies that match your ideal prospect profile and fewer records that only loosely fit your target.

# NAICS Classification & Reference Center

## NAICS guidance for choosing, verifying, and documenting industry classifications

**NAICS classifies business establishments based on their primary economic activity.** Use this reference center to identify the right classification, compare close 6-digit codes, understand code boundaries, and document why a code was selected.

For quick code discovery, start with the NAICS Directory. Use the guidance below when the classification needs closer review or a decision you can explain.

[Browse the NAICS Directory](https://siccode.com/naics-code-lookup-directory)[How to Choose a NAICS Code](https://siccode.com/page/how-to-choose-the-correct-naics-or-sic-code)[What Is a NAICS Code?](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-naics-code)Core classification framework
### NAICS classification at a glance

1.   **1. Identify the establishment**Determine the specific business unit or establishment being classified.
2.   **2. Determine the primary activity**Identify the principal economic activity performed by that establishment.
3.   **3. Compare 6-digit candidates**Check hierarchy fit, definitions, boundaries, and close alternatives.
4.   **4. Document the decision**Record the selected code, evidence used, and why close alternatives were rejected.

### When this page is the right fit

*   Ambiguous or multi-activity businesses
*   Establishment-level classification questions
*   Close-code and included/excluded boundary decisions
*   Repeatable review and documentation standards
*   NAICS governance, revisions, and version control

### Use a more specific resource when needed

[Need to find a code? Use the NAICS Directory](https://siccode.com/naics-code-lookup-directory)[New to NAICS? Start with the beginner guide](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-naics-code)[Need the formal workflow? Use the methodology](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-methodology)

### On this page

*   [NAICS classification in plain language](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#plain-language)
*   [NAICS classification scope and principles](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#classification-scope)
*   [Evidence used to assign a NAICS code](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#classification-evidence)
*   [NAICS code selection and verification workflow](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#code-selection-workflow)
*   [How to interpret NAICS code boundaries](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#code-boundaries)
*   [NAICS classification examples and walkthroughs](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#classification-examples)
*   [Complex NAICS classification scenarios](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#complex-scenarios)
*   [NAICS quality checks and review controls](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#quality-controls)
*   [NAICS revision cycles and versioning](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#versioning)
*   [When to defer to agency-specific NAICS guidance](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#agency-guidance)
*   [Primary NAICS sources](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#primary-sources)
*   [Related NAICS resources](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#related-resources)
*   [NAICS classification questions and answers](https://siccode.com/page/naics-classification-reference-center#questions)

## NAICS classification in plain language

A NAICS code identifies the primary economic activity of an establishment. The starting question is: what activity does this establishment primarily perform?

**Practical shortcut:** for many customer-facing businesses, it can help to ask what customers are mainly paying the establishment to provide. This is a practical clue, not a universal revenue-only rule. 

### Simple version

1.   Describe what the establishment mainly does.
2.   Find the NAICS descriptions that best match that activity.
3.   Compare the most specific 6-digit candidates.
4.   Confirm hierarchy fit and code boundaries.
5.   Record why the selected code fits.

### When classification gets harder

*   The business performs several economically significant activities.
*   Different locations perform different functions.
*   Two similar 6-digit codes both appear plausible.
*   Branding or keywords do not accurately describe the operation.
*   The code affects lending, insurance, procurement, compliance, or reporting.

**Establishment:** usually a single physical location where business is conducted or services are performed. Some physically dispersed activities, including certain construction, transportation, and telecommunications operations, are treated differently under NAICS. See [Establishment-Level vs Company-Level NAICS](https://siccode.com/page/establishment-level-vs-company-level-naics-codes:-how-naics-is-assigned).

**Primary activity**The principal economic activity performed by the establishment.

**Hierarchy**The 2-digit through 6-digit NAICS structure.

**Boundary**What a code covers and what belongs elsewhere.

**Near-neighbor**A similar code that should be compared before final selection.

**Vintage**The NAICS edition/year used for a particular classification record.

## NAICS classification scope and principles

Consistent NAICS assignment starts with the correct unit of analysis, the establishment, and then evaluates its primary economic activity within the NAICS hierarchy.

### Core principles

*   **Establishment scope:** classify the specific operating unit being evaluated.
*   **Primary activity:** select the code that best represents the establishment’s principal economic activity.
*   **Hierarchy fit:** validate the path from sector through the 6-digit national industry.
*   **Boundary logic:** compare definitions, included activities, exclusions, and close alternatives.
*   **Stability control:** do not change codes without a reason such as new evidence, operational change, revision adoption, or error correction.

### What this page is not

*   It is not a replacement for official U.S. NAICS publications or Census reference materials.
*   It is not legal, tax, procurement, insurance, or agency-specific eligibility advice.
*   It is not a keyword-only lookup page. Use the NAICS Directory when search is the main task.

Need the beginner explanation? [Start with What Is a NAICS Code?](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-naics-code)

**Important support-function distinction:** a support activity performed inside a broader operating establishment does not automatically define that establishment’s NAICS code. A separate enterprise-support establishment may, however, have its own classification based on the activity performed there. 

## Evidence used to assign a NAICS code

A defensible classification should be based on what the establishment actually does, not simply its name, brand, website keyword, or self-selected label.

### Common evidence signals

*   Primary activity statements from the business
*   Products or services actually delivered
*   Production process and operating model
*   Customer output and revenue model indicators
*   Revenue, receipts, shipments, employment, payroll, or labor allocation when useful
*   Location function, such as plant, warehouse, headquarters, clinic, store, branch, or support office

### How to evaluate primary activity

Ideally, classification reflects the economic significance of the establishment’s production activity and resources used. In practical classification work, consistent proxies may be needed when the ideal measure is unavailable.

*   **Revenue / receipts:** useful where activity-specific receipts are available.
*   **Labor / employment:** useful where staff time strongly indicates the dominant operation.
*   **Production / operating model:** useful for manufacturing, installation, distribution, care, consulting, and similar distinctions.
*   **Customer output:** useful when the economic product or service is otherwise unclear.

### Why 6 digits matter

2-digit Sector

Broad economic area, such as Construction, Manufacturing, Retail Trade, or Health Care.

3-digit Subsector

Narrows the operating model within the sector.

4-digit Industry Group

Separates more specific types of economic activity.

5-digit NAICS Industry

Often where close-code distinctions become more important.

6-digit National Industry

**Primary verification layer:** use this level for final code fit, boundary review, and detailed comparison.

### Better approach

Classify the establishment by the economic activity it primarily performs, then verify the exact 6-digit boundary.

### Common drift risk

Letting a single keyword such as “pump,” “software,” or “medical” determine the sector without reviewing the full operation.

## NAICS code selection and verification workflow

When several codes appear plausible, the decision should be explicit, repeatable, and easy for another reviewer to understand.

**Rule of thumb:** choose the most specific defensible 6-digit NAICS code whose definition and boundaries best match the establishment’s primary economic activity. 

1.   **Describe the activity:** write one plain-language sentence describing what the establishment primarily does.
2.   **Generate candidates:** identify likely codes from activity evidence, not merely branding or keywords.
3.   **Validate the hierarchy:** confirm that each candidate sits in the correct sector and broader NAICS path.
4.   **Confirm boundaries:** compare definitions, included activities, exclusions, and near-neighbor codes.
5.   **Select specificity:** choose the most specific 6-digit code you can justify.
6.   **Document the why-not:** record why close alternatives were rejected.
7.   **Store version context:** retain the NAICS vintage / edition used for the decision.

Deep dive: determining primary activity when direct revenue detail is unavailable

Use consistent proxies so similar establishments are handled in the same way.

*   **Labor or time proxy:** which activity uses the largest share of employee time?
*   **Operational proxy:** what activity drives production or delivery?
*   **Customer-output proxy:** what product or service is the establishment principally providing?
*   **Stability control:** document the proxy used so the code does not change later without a clear reason.

## How to interpret NAICS code boundaries

Code titles are useful labels, but they are not enough for close classifications. Boundary review is what separates a plausible code from a defensible code.

### Check these elements

*   The official NAICS definition
*   Included activities and examples
*   Excluded activities and cross-references
*   Close 6-digit alternatives
*   The full hierarchy path from sector to national industry

### Do not classify from the title alone

Similar businesses may share words in their names while belonging to different NAICS industries because the production activity, customer output, operating model, or establishment function differs.

For a deeper boundary guide, see [NAICS Included vs Excluded Activities: How to Interpret Code Boundaries](https://siccode.com/page/naics-included-vs-excluded-activities:-how-to-interpret-code-boundaries).

## NAICS classification examples and walkthroughs

These examples show why the same company description can point to different NAICS areas depending on the establishment’s primary economic activity.

### Example 1: Solar business with installation, sales, and consulting

**Business facts:** “Solar Solutions & Consulting Group” installs solar panels, provides energy-efficiency consulting, and sells solar components online.

### Classification question

Which activity is primary at the establishment being classified?

*   If installation dominates, evaluate construction / contractor candidates.
*   If consulting dominates, evaluate professional-services candidates.
*   If product sales dominate, evaluate wholesale, retail, or e-commerce candidates.

### What gets documented

*   The primary activity supported by the evidence
*   Alternative activity types considered
*   Candidate codes reviewed
*   Why the selected boundary fits better than the alternatives

### Example 2: Manufacturer that also distributes products

**Business facts:** “Apex Industrial Sealing Corp” manufactures custom rubber gaskets, distributes third-party seals, and maintains a limited on-site counter for trade customers.

### Classification question

Is production, distribution, or retail activity economically primary at this establishment?

*   Confirm what physically and operationally happens at the location.
*   Compare manufacturing, wholesale, and retail candidates.
*   Do not let “distributor” language override evidence that the establishment primarily manufactures.

### What gets documented

*   Primary production / operating activity
*   Secondary distribution or counter-sales activity
*   Close-code alternatives reviewed
*   Final rationale and effective date

Deep dive: what makes a close-code decision defensible?

*   **Candidate list:** record the plausible code choices.
*   **Evidence:** capture the establishment’s primary activity and supporting signals.
*   **Boundary logic:** explain why the selected code fits better than near-neighbor codes.
*   **Final rationale:** retain a concise written reason for the selected classification.

Example of code-page verification depth: [NAICS 621111 Offices of Physicians](https://siccode.com/naics-code/621111/offices-physicians).

## Complex NAICS classification scenarios

These situations often create inconsistent results across databases. Use the same basic workflow: establish scope, determine primary activity, compare candidates, verify boundaries, and document the result.

### Auxiliary and support activities

A support activity inside an operating establishment does not automatically determine the NAICS code. A separate support establishment may require its own classification.

### Franchisor vs franchisee

Classify local establishments by their actual activity. Do not assume the franchisor entity and every franchisee location share the same classification.

### Digital and platform businesses

Marketplace, software, media, retail, and service models can overlap. Validate the operating model against the actual economic product or service delivered.

### Holding companies and operating units

Parent entities and operating establishments may have different primary activities and therefore different NAICS classifications.

### Seasonal businesses

Activity mix can change during the year. Anchor the decision to the relevant reporting period and document the evidence used.

### Mergers and acquisitions

Re-review classification when a transaction materially changes the establishment’s operations, production, or output. Rebranding alone is not necessarily a classification trigger.

A strong NAICS decision should be reviewable by another person without requiring them to guess how the code was selected.

*   **Parent-child alignment:** does the 6-digit code fit the broader hierarchy?
*   **Near-neighbor check:** were similar codes compared before selection?

# Classification Research Tools: Industry, Product, Occupational Codes & Conversions

Classification codes do not all classify the same thing. NAICS, SIC, ISIC, NACE, UK SIC, ANZSIC, and GICS organize businesses or economic activity by industry. NAPCS, CPC, CPA, HS, CN, and EBOPS organize products, goods, or services. SOC classifies occupations, CIP classifies instructional programs, and identifiers such as UEI, CAGE, and D-U-N-S identify entities or locations rather than industries.

Use this research hub to identify the correct system before choosing a code, compare current versions and jurisdictions, and move between related systems when a crosswalk is needed.

 A classification system answers what kind of activity, product, occupation, or program is being classified. An identifier answers which entity or location is being referenced. Crosswalks connect systems, but they do not make different classifications interchangeable. 

Convert a classification code

## Choose the system by what is being classified

The first step is to identify the object being classified. Using the wrong family of codes can produce a technically valid code that answers the wrong question.

| Question | System family | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What industry or economic activity? | Industry classification | NAICS, SIC, ISIC, NACE, UK SIC, ANZSIC, GICS |
| What product or service? | Product classification | NAPCS, CPC, CPA |
| What good is being imported or exported? | Customs and trade nomenclature | HS, CN |
| What cross-border service is being traded? | International trade in services | EBOPS |
| What occupation or job? | Occupational classification | SOC |
| What field of study or instructional program? | Education classification | CIP |
| Which legal entity, supplier, or facility? | Entity or location identifier | UEI, CAGE, D-U-N-S |
| How does one classification relate to another? | Crosswalk or concordance | NAICS to SIC, SIC to NAICS, NAICS to ISIC, ISIC to NAICS |

## Industry classification systems

Industry classifications organize establishments, companies, or economic activities into defined industry categories. The correct system depends on the jurisdiction, statistical program, business use, or investment context.

| System | What it classifies | Geographic or analytical scope | Current reference as of September 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NAICS](https://siccode.com/naics-code-lookup-directory)North American Industry Classification System | Establishments by primary economic activity in the official statistical framework. | United States, Canada, and Mexico, with national detail. | 2022 NAICS is current in the United States. The 2027 U.S. revision is under development. |
| [SIC](https://siccode.com/sic-code-lookup-directory)Standard Industrial Classification | Industries within the established U.S. SIC framework. | United States business, government, financial, analytical, and historical data contexts. | The 1987 SIC Manual remains the principal official U.S. SIC reference. |
| [ISIC](https://siccode.com/isic-code-lookup-directory)International Standard Industrial Classification | Economic activities using the United Nations international industry framework. | Global statistical comparability. | ISIC Rev. 5 is the current UN revision. |
| [NACE](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code)Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community | Economic activities for European statistical use. | European Union and European Statistical System. | NACE Rev. 2.1 applies to European statistics from reference year 2025 onward. |
| [UK SIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-uk-sic-code)UK Standard Industrial Classification | Economic activities in the United Kingdom. | United Kingdom statistics and administrative uses. | UK SIC 2026 is the current published standard. Implementation timing varies by ONS system and statistical program. |
| [ANZSIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-anzsic-code)Australian and New Zealand Standard Industrial Classification | Economic activities. | Australia and New Zealand. | ANZSIC 2006 Revision 2.0 is the latest ABS release. |
| [GICS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-gics-code)Global Industry Classification Standard | Companies for investment research and capital-markets analysis. | Global investment universe. | Current GICS structure has four levels: Sector, Industry Group, Industry, and Sub-Industry. |

 GICS belongs with industry classification systems, not with entity identifiers. It categorizes companies for investment analysis; it does not uniquely identify a business in the way UEI, CAGE, or D-U-N-S does. 

### Extended NAICS and Extended SIC

Official U.S. NAICS ends at six digits, and official U.S. SIC ends at four digits. SICCODE.com also provides commercial Extended NAICS and Extended SIC detail for more specific business-data segmentation. These extensions preserve the official NAICS or SIC code as the underlying classification anchor but are not additional official government levels.

*   [Extended NAICS Code Directory](https://siccode.com/extended-naics-code-lookup-directory)Commercial detail below the official six-digit U.S. NAICS classification.
*   [Extended SIC Code Directory](https://siccode.com/extended-sic-code-lookup-directory)Commercial detail below the official four-digit U.S. SIC classification.

### NAICS language and national references

French and Spanish NAICS references are national or language presentations within the broader North American classification framework, not unrelated classification systems.

*   [SCIAN Français](https://siccode.com/page/scian-francais)French-language North American industry classification reference.
*   [SCIAN Español](https://siccode.com/page/scian-espanol)Spanish-language North American industry classification reference.

## Product, goods, and services classifications

Product classifications describe what is produced, sold, traded, or supplied. They should not be confused with industry classifications, which describe the economic activity of the establishment or company.

| System | What it classifies | Primary context | Current reference as of September 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [NAPCS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-napcs-code)North American Product Classification System | Goods and services as products. | North American product statistics and economic analysis. | 2022 NAPCS structure is the current U.S. reference. |
| [CPC](https://siccode.com/page/central-product-classification-cpc)Central Product Classification | Goods and services within a comprehensive UN product framework. | International product statistics and economic accounts. | CPC Version 3.0 is the current UN product classification. |
| [CPA](https://siccode.com/page/statistical-cpa)Statistical Classification of Products by Activity | Goods and services linked to economic activities. | European Union product statistics. | CPA Version 2.2 applies to European statistics from reference year 2025 onward. |
| [HS](https://siccode.com/page/harmonized-system-hs)Harmonized System | Goods traded internationally. | Customs tariffs and international merchandise trade statistics. | HS 2022 remains the valid WCO version for current international trade transactions. HS 2028 enters into force on January 1, 2028. |
| [CN](https://siccode.com/page/combined-nomenclature-cn)Combined Nomenclature | Goods for EU customs and trade-statistics purposes. | European Union customs declarations, tariff treatment, and trade statistics. | The 2026 CN applies from January 1, 2026 and is updated annually. |
| [EBOPS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-ebops-extended-balance-of-payments-services-classification)Extended Balance of Payments Services Classification | Cross-border service transactions. | Balance of payments and international trade in services statistics. | EBOPS 2026 is operational and updates EBOPS 2010. |

 HS and CN classify goods for customs and trade purposes. EBOPS classifies cross-border service transactions. NAPCS, CPC, and CPA are product classifications. None of these systems should be used as a substitute for an industry classification merely because a product or service is associated with a particular industry. 

## Occupation and education classifications

Occupation and education codes classify people, jobs, and instructional programs rather than businesses or industries.

| System | What it classifies | Current reference as of September 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [SOC](https://siccode.com/soc-code-lookup-directory)Standard Occupational Classification | Workers and occupations according to occupational definitions. | 2018 SOC remains the current U.S. federal statistical standard. A 2028 SOC revision is underway. |
| [CIP](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-cip-code)Classification of Instructional Programs | Fields of study and instructional programs. | 2020 CIP is the most recent NCES version. |

A company can employ workers from many SOC occupations and can recruit graduates from many CIP programs. Neither SOC nor CIP describes the company's industry.

## Business and entity identifiers

Entity identifiers answer which organization or facility is being referenced. They do not classify what the business does.

| Identifier | What it identifies | Current use | Relationship to industry codes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [UEI](https://sam.gov/)Unique Entity ID | An entity in the U.S. federal award environment. | UEI from SAM.gov has been the authoritative federal entity identifier for federal awards since April 4, 2022. | Identifies the entity. NAICS identifies activity for statistical, contracting, or other program purposes. |
| [CAGE Code](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-cage-code)Commercial and Government Entity Code | A supplier, government organization, or facility at a specific location in federal and defense systems. | Maintained through the Defense Logistics Agency CAGE program and used in procurement and logistics contexts. | Identifies a facility or organization record. It does not describe the facility's industry. |
| [D-U-N-S Number](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-duns-number)Dun & Bradstreet business identifier | A business record in the D&B commercial identity system. | Still used in commercial credit, supplier, onboarding, and business-information workflows. It is no longer the U.S. federal award identifier. | Identifies a business record. NAICS or SIC can separately describe industry activity. |

 UEI replaced D-U-N-S as the U.S. federal award entity identifier in 2022. D-U-N-S remains a commercial business identifier, and CAGE remains a separate federal and defense identifier associated with suppliers, organizations, and specific locations. 

## Crosswalks and classification conversion tools

Crosswalks show relationships between classification systems or between different editions of the same system. They are research tools, not automatic proof that two codes have identical scope. Use the [conversion field](https://siccode.com/page/classification-research-tools-industry-product-occupational-codes-conversions#ct-convert) above to look up a code, or open a dedicated conversion tool below.

*   [NAICS to SIC Conversion](https://siccode.com/naics-to-sic-conversion)Find candidate SIC classifications related to a NAICS code.
*   [SIC to NAICS Conversion](https://siccode.com/sic-to-naics-conversion)Find candidate NAICS classifications related to a SIC code.
*   [NAICS to ISIC Conversion](https://siccode.com/naics-to-isic-conversion)Relate North American industries to the UN international industry framework.
*   [ISIC to NAICS Conversion](https://siccode.com/isic-to-naics-conversion)Relate ISIC classifications to candidate NAICS industries.
*   [NAICS vs SIC Codes](https://siccode.com/page/naics-vs-sic)Compare structure, classification concepts, current use, and mapping limitations.
