# What is a Classification System

Updated: 2026 | [Reviewed By: SICCODE.com Industry Classification Review Team](https://siccode.com/page/industry-classification-review-team) | [Framework: Data Governance & Stewardship Standards](https://siccode.com/page/siccode-data-governance-framework-stewardship-standards-siccode-com)

A classification system is a structured way to group economic activities, products, or goods so data can be collected, compared, and analyzed consistently. It creates a common language that helps businesses, researchers, governments, and institutions organize information in a meaningful way.

In practice, classification systems make it easier to measure how the economy works. They support reporting, benchmarking, trade analysis, market research, compliance, and industry targeting by placing similar activities or products into defined categories.

## Why Classification Systems Matter

*   **They create consistency:** the same type of activity or product can be classified the same way across datasets, reports, and organizations.
*   **They improve analysis:** data becomes easier to compare across industries, regions, and time periods.
*   **They support decision-making:** businesses and institutions can use classification-based data for planning, targeting, forecasting, and regulation.
*   **They provide a common language:** classification standards help different teams and systems work from the same definitions.

## Main Types of Classification Systems

### Economic Activity Classifications

These systems classify what a business or establishment does. They are used to analyze production activity, inputs, labor, capital formation, and related financial activity.

### Product and Goods Classifications

These systems classify the products or goods being produced, sold, traded, or transported. They help analysts study trends in production, trade, consumption, and market movement.

Examples of activity classifications include [NAICS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-naics-code), [SIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-sic-code), [ISIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-isic-code), [UK SIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-uk-sic-code), [ANZSIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-anzsic-code), and [NACE](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code). Examples of product and goods classifications include [HS](https://siccode.com/page/harmonized-system-hs), [NAPCS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-napcs-code), [CPA](https://siccode.com/page/statistical-cpa), and [CPC](https://siccode.com/page/central-product-classification-cpc).

## Classification Systems by Level

| Level | Economic Activities | Products | Goods |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| World Level | [ISIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-isic-code) | [CPC](https://siccode.com/page/central-product-classification-cpc) | [HS](https://siccode.com/page/harmonized-system-hs) |
| North America Level | [NAICS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-naics-code) | [SIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-sic-code) | [NAPCS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-napcs-code) | [NAPCS](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-napcs-code) |
| EU Level | [NACE](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code) | [CPA](https://siccode.com/page/statistical-cpa) | [CN](https://siccode.com/page/combined-nomenclature-cn) |

World-level systems are generally maintained by international statistical bodies. EU-level systems are maintained for European statistical and trade reporting.

## How Activity and Product Classifications Differ

### Activity Classification

Focuses on what an establishment primarily does. This helps analysts study business operations, production inputs, labor use, financial activity, and industry structure.

### Product Classification

Focuses on the goods or services themselves. This helps track production, trade, consumption, transport, and product-level demand across markets.

## Why This Matters for Business Data

Classification systems are not only used in government statistics. They also help businesses organize customer and prospect data, build industry-targeted lists, compare markets, and improve reporting quality.

SICCODE.com focuses on the classification side of business data because better industry understanding leads to better-targeted lists, cleaner segmentation, and more useful analysis than generic providers can usually offer.

## Frequently Used Classification Systems

**NAICS** - North American Industry Classification System used to classify business activities in North America.

**SIC** - Standard Industrial Classification system used to classify industries and business establishments.

**ISIC** - International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities published by the United Nations.

**NACE** - Statistical classification of economic activities in the European Communities.

**CPC** - Central Product Classification used for products and services.

**CPA** - European Classification of Products by Activity.

**HS** - Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System used in trade classification.

**CN** - Combined Nomenclature used in European foreign trade statistics.

**SITC** - Standard International Trade Classification used for trade statistics.

**PRODCOM** - EU goods classification used for statistics on industrial production.

## About SIC 6-Digit Codes

A SIC Code describes the primary business activity of a company. With more than 10,000 unique classifications, SIC codes have been extended to create the most accurate way to target businesses.

Businesses often use SIC codes to identify companies within specific industries for marketing purposes. By determining the SIC code of their best clients, they can use this information to successfully acquire more customers within that industry.

[More About SIC Codes](https://siccode.com/sic-code-lookup-directory)[More About SIC 6-Digit Codes](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-the-difference-between-digit-sic-codes)

## Questions & Answers

*   ### How can I use SIC 6-Digit Codes?

The main usage of SIC 6-digit codes is for target marketing purposes. Whether using the 6-digit system, the 7-digit system, or the 8-digit system, the extended SIC codes offer a more precise targeting option than either the government 4-digit level [SIC](https://siccode.com/sic-code-lookup-directory) or [NAICS](https://siccode.com/naics-code-lookup-directory). While there are currently 1,066 industries in NAICS, there are over 10,000 industry code possibilities using the SIC 6-Digit Codes. When [requesting a business list](https://siccode.com/business-list-usa), feel free to use whichever system is comfortable, as Business Data Specialists are well-versed in the mapping and cross-analysis of each of these systems. This will ensure you get the most precise targeted business list possible.  
*   ### Why were SIC 6-Digit Codes created?

The U.S. Government was aware of certain limitations of the official 4-digit SIC Code System and allowed for the creation and usage of SIC codes by private companies and agencies. The business world seized on the opportunity to extend the SIC Code system and there are currently three separate but relatable SIC code systems in place - 6-digit, 7-digit, and 8-digit systems. The creation of these systems allowed marketers to focus their campaigns on a more precise level and avoid unnecessary costs; while devoting resources to the specific industries that matter. Another benefit of the SIC 6-Digit Code System is the continuous updating of evolving and emerging industries by the Private industry, which occurs at a much quicker pace than the 5-year update of NAICS.

## About ISIC Codes

ISIC is a classification structure of economic activities (industries) based on a set of internationally agreed concepts, definitions, principles and classification rules. ISIC is used to classify statistical units, such as establishments or enterprises, according to the economic activity in which they mainly engage.

ISIC has a central position among existing classifications of economic activities, as well as other economic classifications, such as those for products. ISIC provides the internationally accepted standard for categorizing producing units within an economy, which allows for data comparison at the national and international levels. ISIC is a completely separate classification system from SIC Codes.

[More About ISIC Codes](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-isic-code)[For More About SIC Codes](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-sic-code)

## Questions & Answers

*   ### What is the difference between ISIC codes and SIC Codes?

ISIC is the abbreviation for International Standard Industrial Classification of All Economic Activities whereas SIC is the abbreviation for [Standard Industrial Classification](https://siccode.com/sic-code-lookup-directory). - Both are completely different classification systems, and although comparable at certain levels, are entirely independent from one another. SIC Codes predate ISIC codes and were developed by and for the United States. The ISIC Code system is developed and updated by the United Nations and many countries throughout the world rely on it for their industrial classifications. For business targeting purposes in the United States and Canada, the SIC Code system is the preferred and most precise method available.  
*   ### What are some of the agencies and organizations that use ISIC Codes?

The United Nations, the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and other international bodies use ISIC when publishing and analysing statistical data. A number of countries have utilized ISIC as the basis for developing their national industrial classifications. Many countries have adapted their national industrial activity classifications based on ISIC. With the fourth revision of ISIC, considerable effort was made in strengthening its relevance and comparability with other classifications; such as the [Australian and New Zealand Standard Industrial Classification (ANZSIC)](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-anzsic-code), the General Industrial Classification of Economic Activities within the European Communities (NACE), and the [North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)](https://siccode.com/naics-code-lookup-directory).

# SIC Classification & Reference Center

## SIC guidance for classification, legacy continuity, and defensible recordkeeping

**SIC classifies establishments by their primary industry activity using the official four-digit Standard Industrial Classification structure.** Use this reference center to choose and verify SIC codes, preserve consistency across legacy datasets, understand where SIC is still used, and distinguish official SIC from more granular non-governmental Extended SIC classifications.

For quick code discovery, start with the SIC Directory. Use the guidance below when the decision requires closer review, historical continuity, crosswalk logic, or documentation that another reviewer can follow.

[Browse the SIC Directory](https://siccode.com/sic-code-lookup-directory)[How to Choose a SIC Code](https://siccode.com/page/how-to-choose-the-correct-naics-or-sic-code)[What Is a SIC Code?](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-sic-code)

**Official U.S. reference:** 1987 SIC Manual**Status:** legacy classification still used in selected current workflows**Official SIC depth:** 4 digits

Core classification framework
### SIC classification at a glance

1.   **1. Define the unit**Identify the establishment, location, company entity, or record being classified.
2.   **2. Determine primary activity**Identify the major product, service, or economic activity that best represents the unit.
3.   **3. Verify the 4-digit SIC**Check the hierarchy, industry description, boundaries, and close alternatives.
4.   **4. Preserve the rationale**Record the official SIC, evidence used, and any Extended SIC detail kept separately.

## SIC classification in plain language

A SIC code groups an establishment or business record into an industry based on its primary activity. The practical question is: what major product, service, or economic activity best represents the unit being classified?

### Simple version

1.   Define the establishment, location, company entity, or record being classified.
2.   Describe its primary product, service, or economic activity.
3.   Find the official 4-digit SIC industry that best matches.
4.   Compare nearby codes and industry descriptions before finalizing.
5.   Document the decision so it can be applied consistently later.

### When SIC classification gets harder

*   The business performs several materially different activities.
*   A legacy record uses a broad or inconsistent SIC value.
*   Company-level and establishment-level activities differ.
*   A modern business model does not fit old SIC language neatly.
*   SIC must be reconciled with NAICS or another internal taxonomy.

**Core principle:** the SIC designation is normally based on the primary activity of the establishment. Do not classify from the company name or a single keyword when the operating facts point elsewhere. 

**SIC is a legacy standard, not a periodically updated modern taxonomy.** That makes consistency and documentation especially important when applying SIC to newer business models. 

## Official SIC structure and Extended SIC

Official U.S. SIC is hierarchical and ends at the four-digit industry level. More granular Extended SIC classifications should be treated as an additional non-governmental classification layer, not as official government SIC codes.

Division Letter level

Broad economic division in the official 1987 SIC structure.

2-digit Major Group

Broad industry grouping within the division.

3-digit Industry Group

Narrows the classification within the major group.

4-digit Industry

**Official detailed SIC level:** use this as the government-standard SIC classification.

**Official SIC**
The U.S. Standard Industrial Classification system uses official four-digit industry codes. Government SIC references should be cited and interpreted at this level.

**Extended SIC**
Extended SIC provides more granular business classifications for data, segmentation, research, and targeting. These extensions are non-governmental classifications and should be labeled separately from official four-digit SIC.

Browse the [Extended SIC Code Lookup](https://siccode.com/extended-sic-code-lookup-directory) when you need more detailed classification below the official four-digit industry.

## SIC code selection and verification workflow

When a SIC assignment must remain consistent across teams, records, or review cycles, use an explicit workflow rather than relying on memory, keywords, or historical values alone.

**Rule of thumb:** select the official four-digit SIC industry that best represents the primary activity of the unit being classified, then record any additional Extended SIC detail separately. 

1.   **Define the unit:** establish whether you are classifying an establishment, company entity, location, or legacy record.
2.   **Describe the activity:** write a plain-language statement of the main product, service, or economic activity.
3.   **Generate candidates:** identify plausible official SIC industries from the actual activity.
4.   **Validate hierarchy:** confirm that each candidate fits the correct division, major group, and industry group.
5.   **Check boundaries:** compare industry descriptions and close alternatives.
6.   **Select the official 4-digit SIC:** choose the best defensible industry code.
7.   **Add Extended SIC if needed:** store more granular non-governmental Extended SIC detail separately from official SIC.
8.   **Document the rationale:** retain evidence, rejected alternatives, and any crosswalk assumptions.

### Useful decision evidence

*   Major product or service
*   Primary business activity
*   Revenue or receipts by activity when available
*   Employment, payroll, hours, or operating activity as supporting proxies
*   Location function and establishment scope
*   Historical SIC values and the evidence behind them

### Common classification drift

*   Copying a legacy SIC code without rechecking the current operation
*   Using a company name as the main classification evidence
*   Mixing official SIC and Extended SIC in one field
*   Changing SIC because a different reviewer prefers another keyword match
*   Assuming a SIC-to-NAICS crosswalk is always one-to-one

For the full review workflow, see [SIC Classification Methodology](https://siccode.com/page/sic-classification-methodology).

## How to interpret SIC code boundaries

SIC code titles are useful shortcuts, but classification should be based on the industry description and the actual activity of the unit being coded.

### Check these elements

*   The official four-digit SIC description
*   The division, major group, and industry-group path
*   Products or services named in the industry description
*   Nearby SIC industries that could plausibly fit
*   Whether the business activity has changed since a legacy code was assigned

### Do not classify from a label alone

SIC language reflects the economic structure and terminology of the official SIC era. Modern business names, websites, and service descriptions may not map cleanly to the historical wording, so the actual operation matters more than a single matching term.

**Modern-business caution:** if an activity did not exist in the same form when SIC was last revised, choose the closest defensible official SIC based on the underlying economic activity and document the interpretation rather than presenting a newly invented official SIC code. 

## SIC governance, consistency, and accuracy

Because official SIC is stable and legacy-oriented, the main governance challenge is consistent interpretation across records, reviewers, and time.

### Classification methodology

Use an explainable process for scope, primary activity, candidate selection, boundary review, and final rationale.

[SIC Classification Methodology](https://siccode.com/page/sic-classification-methodology)

### Governance and lineage

Track why a SIC value was assigned, when it changed, whether it is official or extended, and how it maps to other classification systems.

[SIC Data Governance & Versioning](https://siccode.com/page/sic-data-governance-versioning)

### Accuracy and review

Validate hierarchy fit, close-code alternatives, supporting evidence, and consistency across similar records.

[SIC Accuracy Benchmarks](https://siccode.com/page/sic-accuracy-benchmarks)

### Quality checks to apply

*   **Scope check:** is the correct entity or establishment being classified?
*   **Primary-activity check:** does the SIC represent the actual dominant operation?
*   **Hierarchy check:** does the 4-digit SIC fit its broader official structure?
*   **Legacy check:** is an old SIC still accurate for the current operation?
*   **Official/extended check:** are official and non-governmental Extended SIC classifications stored distinctly?

### Documentation to retain

*   Unit being classified
*   Primary activity statement
*   Evidence used
*   Candidate SIC codes considered
*   Rejected alternatives
*   Official 4-digit SIC
*   Extended SIC, when applicable
*   Effective date and reviewer notes

**Practical standard:** another reviewer should be able to understand the SIC assignment without guessing which keyword, historical record, or crosswalk drove the decision. 

## Where SIC is still used today

NAICS replaced SIC as the primary U.S. federal statistical industry classification, but SIC remains active in selected current systems and is widely retained for legacy continuity, historical analysis, and cross-dataset compatibility.

### Current government example: SEC EDGAR

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission continues to display SIC codes in EDGAR company filings. The SEC also uses SIC categories as part of how the Division of Corporation Finance assigns filing-review responsibility.

[SEC Standard Industrial Classification Code List](https://www.sec.gov/search-filings/standard-industrial-classification-sic-code-list)

### Current reference access: OSHA

OSHA maintains a searchable version of the 1987 SIC Manual, including official 2-, 3-, and 4-digit SIC descriptions and structure.

[OSHA Standard Industrial Classification System Search](https://www.osha.gov/data/sic-search)

### Common modern SIC use cases

*   **Financial and investment analysis:** historical portfolio segmentation and long-run comparison.
*   **Insurance and underwriting:** legacy classifications, historical claims analysis, and internal category continuity.
*   **SEC and securities research:** company filing classification and industry-based filing research.
*   **Marketing and business intelligence:** segmentation, targeting, TAM analysis, and compatibility with older databases.
*   **Data engineering:** maintaining SIC fields and reconciling them with NAICS and other taxonomies.
*   **Historical research:** comparing datasets originally published or coded under SIC.

## SIC and NAICS crosswalks

SIC and NAICS were built differently, so conversions are not always one-to-one. Treat a crosswalk as a mapping aid that may require activity-level review, not as proof that two codes are exact equivalents.

### Crosswalk best practices

*   Confirm the underlying business activity before accepting a mapped code.
*   Expect one SIC code to map to multiple NAICS codes in some industries.
*   Expect multiple SIC codes to converge into one NAICS area in other cases.
*   Retain both original and mapped values when lineage matters.
*   Document which crosswalk source and logic were used.

### Conversion tools

Use the SIC-to-NAICS conversion as a starting point, then confirm the business activity on the corresponding detailed code pages.

[SIC to NAICS Conversion](https://siccode.com/sic-to-naics-conversion)

[SIC Codes vs NAICS Codes](https://siccode.com/page/sic-codes-vs-naics-codes)

## SIC history and legacy continuity

SIC remains useful partly because many historical records, reporting systems, internal taxonomies, and business databases were built around it before NAICS became the primary federal statistical standard.

| Topic | What to know | Recommended practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Official reference** | The searchable official SIC reference still commonly used is the 1987 SIC Manual. | Store official four-digit SIC separately from non-governmental Extended SIC. |
| **Historical data** | Many older federal, commercial, and internal datasets were coded under SIC. | Retain original SIC values where historical comparability matters. |
| **Modern classification** | NAICS became the primary federal statistical classification for newer reference periods. | Maintain both systems when workflows require current NAICS plus historical SIC continuity. |
| **Change control** | Official SIC does not have the same regular revision cycle as NAICS. | Focus on consistent application and documented interpretation rather than frequent re-versioning. |

# What Is a NACE Code? European Industry Classification (NACE)

**Updated:** 2026 · **Standard:** NACE Rev. 2 / Rev. 2.1 · **Alignment:** ISIC · **Governance:**[Authority & Trust Hub](https://siccode.com/page/authority-trust-hub-sic-naics-data-governance)

**What is a NACE code?** NACE, the Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community, is the European Union’s official system for classifying economic activities. It is used to support harmonized statistical reporting across EU Member States and aligned economies, while remaining structurally aligned with the UN’s ISIC framework.

NACE is built as a four-level hierarchy. It lets users move from broad economic sections down to more specific activity classes, which is why it is widely used in business registers, official statistics, administrative data, and comparative industry analysis.

Jump to

*   [NACE structure](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#structure)
*   [Visual hierarchy](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#visual)
*   [Global context](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#context)
*   [Worked example](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#example)
*   [Revisions & updates](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#revisions)
*   [Applications](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#applications)
*   [NACE and ISIC](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#alignment)
*   [Countries using NACE](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-a-nace-code#countries)

## Structure of NACE Codes

NACE is organized as a four-level hierarchy that supports analysis from broad economic groupings down to specific activity classes.

*   **Section:** broad economic coverage identified by a letter
*   **Division:** two-digit activities within a section
*   **Group:** three-digit refinements inside a division
*   **Class:** four-digit activity definitions

## Visual Hierarchy

NACE codes are not flat strings. Each level nests into the next, moving from section to class.

Section

Q

Human health and social work activities

→

Division (2-digit)

86

Human health activities

Group (3-digit)

86.2

Medical and dental practice activities

→

Class (4-digit)

86.23

Dental practice activities

## Global Context

NACE is the EU’s activity classification. It is designed to align with ISIC for international comparability, while adding EU-specific detail for European statistical and administrative use.

**ISIC (UN)**
Global reference framework for economic activity classification used to support cross-country comparability.

Aligned to

**NACE (EU)**
European implementation aligned to ISIC, with additional detail to support EU reporting, business registers, and administrative datasets.

## Worked Hierarchy Example

| Level | Code | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section | Q | Human health and social work activities |
| Division | 86 | Human health activities |
| Group | 86.2 | Medical and dental practice activities |
| Class | 86.23 | Dental practice activities |

## NACE Revisions: Rev. 2 and Rev. 2.1

NACE Rev. 2 remains the baseline still seen in many datasets and systems, while NACE Rev. 2.1 is now the official updated classification and is being progressively rolled out across European statistical domains. Rev. 2.1 introduces new concepts and restructures some headings, while preserving continuity where change was not necessary. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

**Revision principle:** updates often change definitions, boundaries, and heading detail more than the overall hierarchical logic. When comparing datasets over time, always store the NACE revision used.

## Applications of NACE Codes

*   European and national statistical reporting
*   Business registers and administrative datasets
*   Economic policy and sectoral analysis
*   Environmental, regulatory, and compliance frameworks that reference activity categories
*   Market research and comparative industry analysis

## NACE and ISIC Alignment

NACE is structurally aligned with the [International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC)](https://siccode.com/page/what-is-an-isic-code). ISIC provides the global reference framework, while NACE provides the EU’s aligned implementation with more European detail. Eurostat’s guidance explicitly positions NACE Rev. 2.1 as aligned to ISIC while preserving its own EU structure and explanatory notes. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

## Countries Using NACE

NACE is used across the European Union for official statistics and is also used or mirrored by aligned European systems and national variants based on the NACE framework. A simple way to present it on this page is to focus on representative examples rather than imply a closed list. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

## Abstract

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
A well-known mechanism through which new protein-coding genes originate is by modification of pre-existing genes, e.g. by duplication or horizontal transfer. In contrast, many viruses generate protein-coding genes _de novo_, via the overprinting of a new reading frame onto an existing (“ancestral”) frame. This mechanism is thought to play an important role in viral pathogenicity, but has been poorly explored, perhaps because identifying the _de novo_ frames is very challenging. Therefore, a new approach to detect them was needed. We assembled a reference set of overlapping genes for which we could reliably determine the ancestral frames, and found that their codon usage was significantly closer to that of the rest of the viral genome than the codon usage of _de novo_ frames. Based on this observation, we designed a method that allowed the identification of _de novo_ frames based on their codon usage with a very good specificity, but intermediate sensitivity. Using our method, we predicted that the Rex gene of _deltaretroviruses_ has originated _de novo_ by overprinting the Tax gene. Intriguingly, several genes in the same genomic region have also originated _de novo_ and encode proteins that regulate the functions of Tax. Such “gene nurseries” may be common in viral genomes. Finally, our results confirm that the genomic GC content is not the only determinant of codon usage in viruses and suggest that a constraint linked to translation must influence codon usage.

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162 "Author Summary")
## Author Summary

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
How does novelty originate in nature? It is commonly thought that new genes are generated mainly by modifications of existing genes (the “tinkering” model). In contrast, we have shown recently that in viruses, numerous genes are generated entirely _de novo_ (“from scratch”). The role of these genes remains underexplored, however, because they are difficult to identify. We have therefore developed a new method to detect genes originated _de novo_ in viral genomes, based on the observation that each viral genome has a unique “signature”, which genes originated _de novo_ do not share. We applied this method to analyze the genes of Human T-Lymphotropic Virus 1 (HTLV1), a relative of the HIV virus and also a major human pathogen that infects about twenty million people worldwide. The life cycle of HTLV1 is finely regulated – it can stay dormant for long periods and can provoke blood cancers (leukemias) after a very long incubation. We discovered that several of the genes of HTLV1 have originated _de novo_. These novel genes play a key role in regulating the life cycle of HTLV1, and presumably its pathogenicity. Our investigations suggest that such “gene nurseries” may be common in viruses.

## Introduction

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Modification of existing genes, such as by duplication or fusion, is a common and well-understood mechanism by which protein-coding genes originate [[1]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Long1), [[2]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Taylor1). In contrast, we have shown that viruses generate many proteins _de novo_ (hereafter called “_de novo_ proteins”) [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1). Preliminary observations indicate that these proteins play an important role in the pathogenicity of viruses [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[5]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), for instance by neutralizing the host interferon response [[6]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-vanKnippenberg1) or antagonizing the host RNA interference [[7]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Strikingly, p19, the only _de novo_ protein characterised both structurally and functionally, has both a previously unknown structural fold and a previously unknown mechanism of action [[7]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Thus, protein innovation seems to be a significant, but poorly understood part of the evolutionary arms race between hosts and their pathogens [[5]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), [8](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Dawkins1),[9](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Meyerson1).

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Studying _de novo_ proteins should thus greatly enhance our understanding of host-pathogen co-evolution and our knowledge of the function and structure of viral proteins [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1)–[[14]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keller1). However, a major bottleneck that prevents the study of such proteins is their identification, which is very challenging. Finding that a viral protein has no detectable sequence homolog does not reliably indicate that it has originated _de novo_, because viral proteins evolve so fast that they can easily diverge in sequence beyond recognition. To circumvent this problem, in our previous work [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1) and in the current study, we focused on a special case of _de novo_ proteins: those generated by overprinting. Overprinting is a process in which mutations in a protein-coding reading frame allow the expression of a second reading frame while preserving the expression of the first one ([Figure 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g001)), leading to an overlapping gene arrangement [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). It is thought that most overlapping genes evolve by this mechanism, and that consequently each gene overlap contains one ancestral frame and one originated _de novo_[[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). Because overlapping genes are particularly abundant in viruses [[15]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath2)–[[17]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Chirico1), they constitute a rich source of _de novo_ proteins.

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)

[![Image 17: thumbnail](link_12)](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article/figure/image?size=medium&id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162.g001 [link_18] "Click for larger image")

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Identifying which frame is ancestral and which one is _de novo_ (the “genealogy” of the overlap) can be done, in principle, by examining their phylogenetic distribution (the frame with the most restricted distribution is assumed to be the _de novo_ one). ## Abstract

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
A well-known mechanism through which new protein-coding genes originate is by modification of pre-existing genes, e.g. by duplication or horizontal transfer. In contrast, many viruses generate protein-coding genes _de novo_, via the overprinting of a new reading frame onto an existing (“ancestral”) frame. This mechanism is thought to play an important role in viral pathogenicity, but has been poorly explored, perhaps because identifying the _de novo_ frames is very challenging. Therefore, a new approach to detect them was needed. We assembled a reference set of overlapping genes for which we could reliably determine the ancestral frames, and found that their codon usage was significantly closer to that of the rest of the viral genome than the codon usage of _de novo_ frames. Based on this observation, we designed a method that allowed the identification of _de novo_ frames based on their codon usage with a very good specificity, but intermediate sensitivity. Using our method, we predicted that the Rex gene of _deltaretroviruses_ has originated _de novo_ by overprinting the Tax gene. Intriguingly, several genes in the same genomic region have also originated _de novo_ and encode proteins that regulate the functions of Tax. Such “gene nurseries” may be common in viral genomes. Finally, our results confirm that the genomic GC content is not the only determinant of codon usage in viruses and suggest that a constraint linked to translation must influence codon usage.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162 "Author Summary")
## Author Summary

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
How does novelty originate in nature? It is commonly thought that new genes are generated mainly by modifications of existing genes (the “tinkering” model). In contrast, we have shown recently that in viruses, numerous genes are generated entirely _de novo_ (“from scratch”). The role of these genes remains underexplored, however, because they are difficult to identify. We have therefore developed a new method to detect genes originated _de novo_ in viral genomes, based on the observation that each viral genome has a unique “signature”, which genes originated _de novo_ do not share. We applied this method to analyze the genes of Human T-Lymphotropic Virus 1 (HTLV1), a relative of the HIV virus and also a major human pathogen that infects about twenty million people worldwide. The life cycle of HTLV1 is finely regulated – it can stay dormant for long periods and can provoke blood cancers (leukemias) after a very long incubation. We discovered that several of the genes of HTLV1 have originated _de novo_. These novel genes play a key role in regulating the life cycle of HTLV1, and presumably its pathogenicity. Our investigations suggest that such “gene nurseries” may be common in viruses.

## Introduction

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Modification of existing genes, such as by duplication or fusion, is a common and well-understood mechanism by which protein-coding genes originate [[1]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Long1), [[2]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Taylor1). In contrast, we have shown that viruses generate many proteins _de novo_ (hereafter called “_de novo_ proteins”) [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1). Preliminary observations indicate that these proteins play an important role in the pathogenicity of viruses [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[5]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), for instance by neutralizing the host interferon response [[6]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-vanKnippenberg1) or antagonizing the host RNA interference [[7]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Strikingly, p19, the only _de novo_ protein characterised both structurally and functionally, has both a previously unknown structural fold and a previously unknown mechanism of action [[7]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Thus, protein innovation seems to be a significant, but poorly understood part of the evolutionary arms race between hosts and their pathogens [[5]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), [8](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Dawkins1),[9](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Meyerson1).

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Studying _de novo_ proteins should thus greatly enhance our understanding of host-pathogen co-evolution and our knowledge of the function and structure of viral proteins [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[10]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1)–[[14]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keller1). However, a major bottleneck that prevents the study of such proteins is their identification, which is very challenging. Finding that a viral protein has no detectable sequence homolog does not reliably indicate that it has originated _de novo_, because viral proteins evolve so fast that they can easily diverge in sequence beyond recognition. To circumvent this problem, in our previous work [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1) and in the current study, we focused on a special case of _de novo_ proteins: those generated by overprinting. Overprinting is a process in which mutations in a protein-coding reading frame allow the expression of a second reading frame while preserving the expression of the first one ([Figure 1](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g001)), leading to an overlapping gene arrangement [[10]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). It is thought that most overlapping genes evolve by this mechanism, and that consequently each gene overlap contains one ancestral frame and one originated _de novo_[[10]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). Because overlapping genes are particularly abundant in viruses [[15]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath2)–[[17]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Chirico1), they constitute a rich source of _de novo_ proteins.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)

[![Image 11: thumbnail](link_55)](https://doi.org/10.1371/article/figure/image?size=medium&id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162.g001 [link_56] "Click for larger image")

 Download: 
*   [PNG larger image](link_57)
*   [TIFF original image](link_58)

Figure 1.  Rationale for our approach.

[https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162.g001](link_59)

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Identifying which frame is ancestral and which one is _de novo_ (the “genealogy” of the overlap) can be done, in principle, by examining their phylogenetic distribution (the frame with the most restricted distribution is assumed to be the _de novo_ one). One can exclude the possibility that the phylogenetically restricted frame is in fact present in other genomes but has diverged beyond recognition, by checking that outside of its clade, the ancestral frame is not overlapped by any reading frame [[4]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1). This approach is simple and reliable [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1), but is not applicable to cases where the homologs of both frames have an identical phylogenetic distribution. For instance, it could identify the _de novo_ frame in only a minority (40%) of overlaps in our previous study [[3]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1). Therefore, a new method is needed to identify the _de novo_ proteins in most overlapping genes.

[](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
The approach we investigated is based on the hypothesis that the ancestral frame should have a pattern of codon usage (i.e. which synonymous codon(s) is preferred to encode each amino acid [[18]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Plotkin1)) closer to that of the rest of the viral genome than the _de novo_ frame [[10]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). Indeed, analyses of plant RNA viruses and animal DNA viruses [[19]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Adams1), [[20]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Shackelton1) have shown that, within a given viral genome, genes generally have a similar pattern of codon usage, which is thought to depend on the overall GC content of the genome [[19]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Adams1)–[[21]](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Jenkins1). Research Ar ticle

Characterising planktonic dinoflagellate diversity in Singapore
using DNA metabarcoding
Yue Sze1, Lilibeth N. Miranda2, Tsai Min Sin2,†, Danwei Huang1,2

1  Department of Biological Sciences, National University of Singapore, Singapore 117558, Singapore.
2  Tropical Marine Science Institute, National University of Singapore, Singapore 119227, Singapore.
†  Deceased.

Corresponding author: Danwei Huang (huangdanwei@nus.edu.sg)

Academic editor: Thorsten Stoeck  |  Received 19 March 2018|  Accepted 24 April 2018|  Published 17 May 2018

Abstract
Dinoflagellates  are  traditionally  identified  morphologically  using  microscopy,  which  is  a  time-consuming  and  labour-intensive
process.  Hence,  we  explored  DNA  metabarcoding  using  high-throughput  sequencing  as  a  more  efficient  way  to  study  planktonic
dinoflagellate  diversity  in  Singapore’s  waters.  From  29  minimally  pre-sorted  water  samples  collected  at  four  locations  in  western
Singapore,  DNA  was  extracted,  amplified  and  sequenced  for  a  313-bp  fragment  of  the  V4–V5  region  in  the  18S  ribosomal  RNA
gene. Two sequencing runs generated 2,847,170 assembled paired-end reads, corresponding to 573,176 unique sequences. Sequenc-
es  were  clustered  at  97%  similarity  and  analysed  with  stringent  thresholds  (≥150  bp,  ≥20  reads,  ≥95%  match  to  dinoflagellates),
recovering  28  dinoflagellate  taxa.  Dinoflagellate  diversity  captured  includes  parasitic  and  symbiotic  groups  which  are  difficult  to
identify  morphologically.  Richness  is  similar  between  the  inner  and  outer West  Johor  Strait,  but  variations  in  community  structure
are apparent, likely driven by environmental differences. None of the taxa detected in a recent phytoplankton bloom along the West
Johor  Strait  have  been  recovered  in  our  samples,  suggesting  that  background  communities  are  distinct  from  bloom  communities.
The voluminous data obtained in this study contribute baseline information for Singapore’s phytoplankton communities and prompt
future research and monitoring to adopt the approach established here.

Key Words

high-throughput sequencing; Johor Strait; molecular operational taxonomic unit; phytoplankton; Singapore Strait

#### About

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/advantages)

![Image 12](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What is the advantage of using Semantic Scholar instead of other academic search engines?

Semantic Scholar is a free, AI-powered search and discovery tool that helps researchers discover and understand scientific literature that's most relevant to their work.  
  
Semantic Scholar uses machine learning techniques to extract meaning and identify connections from within papers, then surfaces these insights to help scholars gain an in-depth understanding quickly.  
  
Our mission is to accelerate scientific breakthroughs by using AI to help scholars locate and understand the right research, make important connections, and overcome information overload.  
  
If you're a new user, check out our [tutorials](https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/tutorials).

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/open-data)

![Image 13](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

Does Semantic Scholar offer programmatic access to its data through an API or downloadable dataset?

Semantic Scholar is committed to supporting high-impact research and engineering by providing universities and organizations with access to our data.  
  
For information about programmatic access to Semantic Scholar's data, please visit:

*   Semantic Scholar Academic Graph (S2AG) RESTful API at [www.semanticscholar.org/product/api](https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/api)
*   Semantic Scholar Academic Graph (S2AG) downloadable datasets updated monthly at [api.semanticscholar.org/corpus](https://api.semanticscholar.org/corpus/)
*   Academic Conference Peer Review Service at [api.semanticscholar.org/api-docs/peer-review](https://api.semanticscholar.org/api-docs/peer-review)
*   S2ORC, a general-purpose corpus for NLP and text mining, at [github.com/allenai/s2orc](https://github.com/allenai/s2orc)

We request that any published research using this data provides proper citing.  
  
Additionally, please visit our [Research page](https://research.semanticscholar.org/publications) to view projects that contribute to some of the features you use on Semantic Scholar. Below each project are links to papers, demos, and GitHub repositories that host datasets, software, and code.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/index-size)

![Image 14](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How many articles does Semantic Scholar currently index?

Our corpus is constantly expanding. See the search bar to get the current number of articles.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/permission-to-use)

![Image 15](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

I would like permission to use, publish, or distribute part of a paper for my work.

In order to obtain permission to use, publish, or distribute any part of a paper listed on our site, please contact the author or publisher directly.  
  
Semantic Scholar is an academic search engine and we are unable to provide the proper permissions on behalf of the authors and publishers whose content is discoverable on our site.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/browser-support)

![Image 16](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

Which browsers does Semantic Scholar support?

We support the latest versions of the most popular browsers including desktop and mobile versions of Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, and Apple Safari. If you discover an issue in your browser, [please contact us](https://www.semanticscholar.org/about/contact).

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/mobile)

![Image 17](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

Is Semantic Scholar available as a mobile application?

We currently do not have a smartphone app, but www.semanticscholar.org is designed to be easily accessed on both desktop and mobile devices.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/endorsement)

![Image 18](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

Does Semantic Scholar support any claims made within research papers found on the site?

Semantic Scholar does not endorse or support any claims made within any papers currently available on the site. As an academic search engine and discovery tool, Semantic Scholar is not engaged in any editorial decisions in the publishing process.  
  
The goal of Semantic Scholar is to leverage AI research and engineering to utilize methods from data mining, natural-language processing, and computer vision to help researchers discover and understand scientific papers.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/beta)

![Image 19](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What is a "Beta" feature?

A Beta feature is one that we make available early while our engineers are still actively working on it. Beta features often still have rough edges and continue to evolve quickly, and we especially welcome feedback on them.  
  
To get exclusive access to new features and to help us shape the future of scholarly research, we invite you to join our [Beta Program](https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/beta-program).

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/tldr)

![Image 20](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What is a TLDR?

A TLDR is an AI-generated summarization for a scientific paper that helps researchers quickly determine the key important aspects of a paper. These extreme paper summaries are an alternative to abstracts, intended to help researchers navigate and understand scientific literature easily and efficiently.  
  
TLDRs are currently limited to the computer science and biomedical domains.   
To find out more about TLDRs, see our [TLDR page](https://www.semanticscholar.org/product/tldr), try our [demo](https://scitldr.apps.allenai.org/), or read the [paper](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/38b6a68aa0554c7fd51dc2c82c76ae804d4cf87d) on Semantic Scholar.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/libraries)

![Image 21](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How does Semantic Scholar support libraries?

For information on how Semantic Scholar can help your researchers, please visit our [Librarian Resources](https://www.semanticscholar.org/about/librarians) page.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/how-does-semantic-scholar-determine-a-papers-field-of-study)

![Image 22](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How does Semantic Scholar determine a paper’s Field of Study?

Semantic Scholar assigns Field of Study using a machine learning classification model based on a paper’s title and abstract. A paper may be assigned up to three Fields of Study.

Field of Study classification is currently limited to English-language papers. It is most reliable when both title and abstract are available, but works on just titles as well. If a paper’s title is too ambiguous, it may not be assigned any Field of Study.

To learn more about Field of Study classification on Semantic Scholar, see our [blog post](https://medium.com/ai2-blog/announcing-s2fos-an-open-source-academic-field-of-study-classifier-9d2f641949e5).

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/integration-with-zotero)

![Image 23](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

Does Semantic Scholar support integration with Zotero?

Yes, you can use [Zotero](https://www.zotero.org/) in multiple ways on Semantic Scholar:

*   **Semantic Reader**: You can save any paper in Semantic Reader. By selecting the Zotero extension on your browser, the paper information, URL, PDF, and TLDR (if available) will be sorted and saved to your Zotero library. You can then easily reopen a paper in Semantic Reader from Zotero and read with AI-powered augmentations such as citation cards.
*   **Paper page**: You can save any paper on any paper page. By selecting the Zotero extension on your browser, the paper information, URL, PDF (if available), and TLDR (if available) will be sorted and saved to your Zotero library.
*   **Search results page**: You can bulk save multiple papers on any search results page. By selecting the Zotero extension on your browser and selecting the paper(s) you want to save on that page, the paper information, URL, PDF (if available), and TLDR (if available) will all be sorted and saved to your Zotero library.

#### Account

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/benefit)

![Image 24](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What are the benefits of creating an account?

Creating a Semantic Scholar account enables you to:

*   Create email alerts for new papers.
*   Generate research feeds for new paper recommendations.
*   Save papers that you'd like to revisit in a library.
*   Claim an author page so you can better manage your author details and papers.

Please note that you do not need to create an account to access papers on Semantic Scholar.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/create-account)

![Image 25](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How do I create an account on Semantic Scholar?

To create a Semantic Scholar account:

1.   Visit any page on the Semantic Scholar site at [www.semanticscholar.org](https://www.semanticscholar.org/).
2.   In the top right corner, select **Create Free Account**.
3.   In the pop-up window, select how you’d like to create an account using your institutional email, Google, Facebook, or your email and password.
4.   Enter your sign-in credentials.

Please note that Semantic Scholar does not collect any sign-in information such as username or password. You do not need to create an account to access papers on Semantic Scholar.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/institutional-login)

![Image 26](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How do I sign in with my institution?

Semantic Scholar partners with Open Athens to provide a privacy-focused institutional sign-in option.  
  
To see if your institution is currently supported, select **Sign In with Your Institution** during sign-in or when creating a free account and search for your organization.

When signed in with your institution, you can access full-text articles that your institution subscribes to. For more details, see [How do I access a PDF using my institutional affiliation?](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq#institutional-access)

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/sign-in)

![Image 27](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

I'm having trouble signing in to my Semantic Scholar account.

**Starting from April 27th, 2023, we no longer support Twitter-authenticated accounts.**

**Starting from December 11th, 2024, we no longer support Facebook-authenticated accounts.**

Semantic Scholar does not collect sign-in information.

*   If you created an account using your [Google](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/41078) credentials, see their password recovery options.
*   If you created an institutional account, contact the institution.
*   If you created an account using an email address and password, select the **Forgot Password** link on the Sign In page.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/forgot-password)

![Image 28](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

I forgot my password and I cannot sign in.

Semantic Scholar does not collect emails and passwords.  
  
If you created an account using a sign-in provider such as Google, Facebook, or your institution, please reach out to the sign-in provider you used when creating your account.  
  
If you did not create your account using any of our sign-in providers, select the **Forgot Password** link and follow the prompts.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/manage-email-preferences)

![Image 29](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How do I manage my email preferences?

To manage your email preferences:

1.   Sign in to your Semantic Scholar account.
2.   Under 'Account' in the top right corner, select **Settings** from the dropdown menu.
3.   Under 'Settings,' go to **Contact Preferences**.
4.   From here, you can disable any existing subscription by sliding the toggle next to the listed options. You may also select **Unsubscribe from all subscriptions** if you no longer wish to receive updates.

You can also access and edit your alert preferences by selecting the **Manage Preferences** link located in the footer of the emails you receive from Semantic Scholar.

#### AI-Features

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/what-should-i-be-cautious-of-when-using-paper-question-answering)

![Image 30](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What should I be cautious of when using features that employ generative AI?

Since text in these features is generated by a language model, it will not be free of errors, and the errors could be difficult to detect. Possible errors include:

*   Factual inaccuracies. Most of these will be subtle, but some may be serious factual errors
*   Awkwardly phrased answers
*   Irrelevant information

While we generally found models to be accurate, you should verify the accuracy of generated text whenever possible.

Features that use generative AI include:

*   Ask This Paper
*   Generative Term Understanding

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/how-are-questions-answered-by-paper-question-answering)

![Image 31](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How are questions answered by Ask This Paper?

We query OpenAI’s gpt3.5-turbo-16k with the content of the current paper alongside your question; the model returns an answer, along with one or more supporting statements from the paper. We find the closest text to snippets in the original paper and display it to you alongside the model answer.

Note that our system has only been tested on English-language papers and is available on a subset of papers.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/what-kinds-of-questions-can-paper-question-answering-handle)

![Image 32](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

What kinds of questions can Ask This Paper handle?

Ask This Paper is designed to work on questions which can be answered by the current paper. There are a few predefined questions that we find generally work well, however, we encourage you to try new questions. We are always learning more about the abilities of this experimental system.

Questions you can try:

*   What is the goal of this paper?
*   What are the key results of this paper?
*   What methods are used?
*   How is the system evaluated?
*   What is the baseline condition?
*   How did the paper differentiate the proposed approach with prior work?

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/how-are-terms-defined-in-the-semantic-reader)

![Image 33](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/605236bb767e9a5bb229c63c/61a6aaf19c62e994c4bc92a2_arrow_grey.svg)

How are terms defined in the Semantic Reader?

When you click on an underlined term in the Semantic Reader, we ask ChatGPT to provide a definition for the given term in the context it appears in.

[Text Link](https://www.semanticscholar.org/faq/which-terms-are-definable-in-the-semantic-reader)

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162 "Abstract")
## Abstract

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
A well-known mechanism through which new protein-coding genes originate is by modification of pre-existing genes, e.g. by duplication or horizontal transfer. In contrast, many viruses generate protein-coding genes _de novo_, via the overprinting of a new reading frame onto an existing (“ancestral”) frame. This mechanism is thought to play an important role in viral pathogenicity, but has been poorly explored, perhaps because identifying the _de novo_ frames is very challenging. Therefore, a new approach to detect them was needed. We assembled a reference set of overlapping genes for which we could reliably determine the ancestral frames, and found that their codon usage was significantly closer to that of the rest of the viral genome than the codon usage of _de novo_ frames. Based on this observation, we designed a method that allowed the identification of _de novo_ frames based on their codon usage with a very good specificity, but intermediate sensitivity. Using our method, we predicted that the Rex gene of _deltaretroviruses_ has originated _de novo_ by overprinting the Tax gene. Intriguingly, several genes in the same genomic region have also originated _de novo_ and encode proteins that regulate the functions of Tax. Such “gene nurseries” may be common in viral genomes. Finally, our results confirm that the genomic GC content is not the only determinant of codon usage in viruses and suggest that a constraint linked to translation must influence codon usage.

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162 "Author Summary")
## Author Summary

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
How does novelty originate in nature? It is commonly thought that new genes are generated mainly by modifications of existing genes (the “tinkering” model). In contrast, we have shown recently that in viruses, numerous genes are generated entirely _de novo_ (“from scratch”). The role of these genes remains underexplored, however, because they are difficult to identify. We have therefore developed a new method to detect genes originated _de novo_ in viral genomes, based on the observation that each viral genome has a unique “signature”, which genes originated _de novo_ do not share. We applied this method to analyze the genes of Human T-Lymphotropic Virus 1 (HTLV1), a relative of the HIV virus and also a major human pathogen that infects about twenty million people worldwide. The life cycle of HTLV1 is finely regulated – it can stay dormant for long periods and can provoke blood cancers (leukemias) after a very long incubation. We discovered that several of the genes of HTLV1 have originated _de novo_. These novel genes play a key role in regulating the life cycle of HTLV1, and presumably its pathogenicity. Our investigations suggest that such “gene nurseries” may be common in viruses.

## Introduction

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Modification of existing genes, such as by duplication or fusion, is a common and well-understood mechanism by which protein-coding genes originate [[1]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Long1), [[2]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Taylor1). In contrast, we have shown that viruses generate many proteins _de novo_ (hereafter called “_de novo_ proteins”) [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1). Preliminary observations indicate that these proteins play an important role in the pathogenicity of viruses [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[5]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), for instance by neutralizing the host interferon response [[6]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-vanKnippenberg1) or antagonizing the host RNA interference [[7]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Strikingly, p19, the only _de novo_ protein characterised both structurally and functionally, has both a previously unknown structural fold and a previously unknown mechanism of action [[7]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Vargason1). Thus, protein innovation seems to be a significant, but poorly understood part of the evolutionary arms race between hosts and their pathogens [[5]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Li1), [8](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Dawkins1),[9](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Meyerson1).

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Studying _de novo_ proteins should thus greatly enhance our understanding of host-pathogen co-evolution and our knowledge of the function and structure of viral proteins [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1)–[[14]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keller1). However, a major bottleneck that prevents the study of such proteins is their identification, which is very challenging. Finding that a viral protein has no detectable sequence homolog does not reliably indicate that it has originated _de novo_, because viral proteins evolve so fast that they can easily diverge in sequence beyond recognition. To circumvent this problem, in our previous work [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1) and in the current study, we focused on a special case of _de novo_ proteins: those generated by overprinting. Overprinting is a process in which mutations in a protein-coding reading frame allow the expression of a second reading frame while preserving the expression of the first one ([Figure 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g001)), leading to an overlapping gene arrangement [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). It is thought that most overlapping genes evolve by this mechanism, and that consequently each gene overlap contains one ancestral frame and one originated _de novo_[[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). Because overlapping genes are particularly abundant in viruses [[15]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath2)–[[17]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Chirico1), they constitute a rich source of _de novo_ proteins.

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
Identifying which frame is ancestral and which one is _de novo_ (the “genealogy” of the overlap) can be done, in principle, by examining their phylogenetic distribution (the frame with the most restricted distribution is assumed to be the _de novo_ one). One can exclude the possibility that the phylogenetically restricted frame is in fact present in other genomes but has diverged beyond recognition, by checking that outside of its clade, the ancestral frame is not overlapped by any reading frame [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1). This approach is simple and reliable [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), [[4]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Sabath1), but is not applicable to cases where the homologs of both frames have an identical phylogenetic distribution. For instance, it could identify the _de novo_ frame in only a minority (40%) of overlaps in our previous study [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1). Therefore, a new method is needed to identify the _de novo_ proteins in most overlapping genes.

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
The approach we investigated is based on the hypothesis that the ancestral frame should have a pattern of codon usage (i.e. which synonymous codon(s) is preferred to encode each amino acid [[18]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Plotkin1)) closer to that of the rest of the viral genome than the _de novo_ frame [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1). Indeed, analyses of plant RNA viruses and animal DNA viruses [[19]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Adams1), [[20]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Shackelton1) have shown that, within a given viral genome, genes generally have a similar pattern of codon usage, which is thought to depend on the overall GC content of the genome [[19]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Adams1)–[[21]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Jenkins1). In overlapping genes, the ancestral frame, which has co-evolved over a long period with the other viral genes, is expected to have a codon usage similar to that of the rest of the genome ([Figure 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g001)). On the other hand, the _de novo_ frame, at birth, will have a codon usage in effect randomized by the shift and thus unlikely to be close to that of the genome. In addition, constraints imposed by the ancestral frame might prevent the _de novo_ frame from adopting, later, the typical genomic codon usage. Consequently, the _de novo_ frame is expected to have a codon usage less similar to that of the viral genome than the ancestral frame ([Figure 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g001)). This approach has been empirically used to try and identify the _de novo_ frame in a number of cases, as have been related methods which rely on the frequency on nucleotides at some or all codon positions [[10]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Keese1), [[22]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Ding1)–[[29]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Lee1). However, the reliability or accuracy of these methods has never been tested. Here we gathered a reference (“benchmark”) dataset composed of overlaps with known genealogy, and used it to answer the following questions: do _de novo_ frames have a codon usage distinguishable from ancestral frames? If yes, can codon usage be used to identify the _de novo_ frame? What is the reliability of the method and its sensitivity? Finally, we applied this method to overlapping genes whose genealogy was undeterminable by the phylogenetic method.

## Results

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162 "A benchmark dataset of overlapping genes with known genealogy")
### A benchmark dataset of overlapping genes with known genealogy

[](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162)
As described in Material and Methods, we assembled a dataset of 27 independent, experimentally proven overlapping genes longer than 140 nt ([Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-t001)). 16 of them have been described previously [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), as indicated by an asterisk in [Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-t001), and 11 additional overlaps were collected for this study. The 27 overlaps come from 25 genera, distributed in 16 viral families covering a wide range of viruses ([Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-t001)). 18 overlaps involve one gene being completely overlapped by the other, while in 9 the overlap is partial (e.g. [Figure 2](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-g002)). All overlapping genes are in the same orientation, i.e. there are no antiparallel overlapping genes in the dataset. To identify the genealogy of the overlaps, we used the same stringent criterion as in our previous study [[3]](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162-Rancurel1), selecting only cases in which one frame, predicted ancestral, had a much wider taxonomic distribution than the other frame, predicted _de novo_. To be confident about the taxonomic distribution of each frame, we carried out extensive searches involving the most up to date similarity search tools, supplemented by in-depth manual searches using contextual information (see Material and Methods). The taxonomic distribution of each frame, and the corresponding evidence, are presented in Supplementary [Table S1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi.1003162.s001). Our predictions of ancestry are supported by functional data: almost all proteins encoded by a frame identified as ancestral have a function central to the viral cycle (such as capsid or replication), while most proteins identified as _de novo_ have a “secondary” function related to pathogenicity (such as silencing suppressor or apoptotic factor) ([Table 1](https://journals.plos.org/ploscompbiol/article?id=10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003162#pcbi-1003162-t001)). Thus, the predicted genealogy of the overlapping genes of the dataset is highly reliable.
